parts.problemMd:
Explore how Mungoshi vividly conveys the beauty and energy of the natural world in ‘Before the Sun’.

Support your ideas with details from the text.

*Before the Sun*

Intense blue morning
promising early heat
and later in the afternoon,
heavy rain.

The bright chips
fly from the sharp axe
for some distance through the air,
arc,
and eternities later,
settle down in showers
on the dewy grass.

It is a big log:
but when you are fourteen
big logs
are what you want.

The wood gives off
a sweet nose-cleansing odour
which (unlike sawdust)
doesn't make one sneeze.

It sends up a thin spiral
of smoke which later straightens
and flutes out
to the distant sky: a signal
of some sort,
or a sacrificial prayer.

The wood hisses,
The sparks fly.

And when the sun
finally shows up
in the East like some
latecomer to a feast
I have got two cobs of maize
ready for it.

I tell the sun to come share
with me the roasted maize
and the sun just winks
like a grown-up.

So I go ahead, taking big
alternate bites:
one for the sun,
one for me.
This one for the sun,
this one for me:
till the cobs
are just two little skeletons
in the sun.

(Charles Mungoshi)
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In ‘Before the Sun’, Charles Mungoshi vividly conveys the beauty and energy of the natural world by presenting it through the heightened perceptions of a fourteen-year-old speaker. Through rich sensory imagery, playful personification, and a tone of youthful wonder, Mungoshi shows how nature becomes a source of joy, energy, and companionship.

From the opening lines, Mungoshi immediately evokes the beauty of the natural world through colour and atmosphere. The morning is described as “Intense blue”, a phrase that conveys both the purity and the strength of the sky’s colour. The day “promising early heat” suggests nature’s generosity, as though the morning is alive with potential. This sense of promise is deepened by the anticipation of “heavy rain” later, capturing the energetic unpredictability of the natural world. In this way, Mungoshi presents nature as dynamic and changeable, filled with movement even before anything happens physically in the poem.

The poet then brings the scene to life through vivid imagery as the speaker chops wood. The “bright chips” that “fly from the sharp axe” create a sense of explosive energy. The verbs “fly”, “arc”, and “settle” emphasise how each action ripples through the environment. The phrase “eternities later” introduces a childlike exaggeration that highlights how closely and intensely the speaker is observing nature; small moments feel stretched and magnified. The detail that the chips fall “in showers / on the dewy grass” merges the boy’s physical effort with the natural world’s beauty. Dew, grass, motion, and light all blend into a single image of freshness and brilliance.

The poem’s middle section focuses on the beauty of nature. The log releases a “sweet nose-cleansing odour”, a description that suggests both freshness and purity. The parenthetical comparison to sawdust “which… doesn’t make one sneeze” adds a humorous, conversational tone, reinforcing the boy’s direct sensory engagement with his environment. Nature is immersive: it can be smelled, touched, and experienced fully. The wood also produces a “thin spiral / of smoke” that rises and “straightens / and flutes out / to the distant sky”. The verb “flutes” gives the smoke elegance and musicality, turning it into a graceful bridge between earth and sky. The idea that the smoke might be a “signal” or “sacrificial prayer” hints at the spiritual possibilities of nature. Even a simple act like burning wood becomes part of a larger, mysterious conversation between the human world and the natural world.

The energy of nature is shown not only through beauty but also through movement and sound: “The wood hisses, / The sparks fly.” The hissing and the flying sparks create an atmosphere of activity and life, almost as though the fire itself is alive. This reinforces the sense that nature is animated, responsive, and dynamic. The boy at the centre of the poem does not control his environment; he participates in it, and the natural world responds in a series of vivid, sensory bursts.

When the sun appears “like some / latecomer to a feast”, Mungoshi introduces gentle humour and personification. The simile transforms the sun into a familiar, almost human figure, suggesting that the natural world is part of the speaker’s social world. The speaker prepares “two cobs of maize” and invites the sun to “come share / with me”, treating it as a companion. The sun “winks / like a grown-up”, reinforcing the playful relationship between child and nature. This interaction is full of imagination and youthful delight, revealing how the natural world becomes a partner in the boy’s moment of joy, rather than something distant or passive.

The final scene, where the speaker eats the maize in alternating bites, “one for the sun, / one for me”, expresses a sense of harmony between human and nature. The shared meal suggests reciprocity and companionship, even though the “sharing” exists only in the child’s imagination. By the end, the cobs become “two little skeletons / in the sun”, an image that blends natural decay with the bright, warm presence of daylight. This closing detail shows how nature and human action leave marks on each other, completing a cycle of energy and transformation.

Overall, Mungoshi vividly conveys nature’s beauty and energy by presenting it through a child’s delighted senses. Through rich imagery, playful personification, and a tone of freshness and freedom, the poem celebrates the vibrancy of the natural world and the joy of being fully alive within it.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is a 25-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 8) because it sustains personal and evaluative engagement and responds critically to the poem and question.
>

parts.problemMd:
How does Philips powerfully express her views on marriage and independence in ‘A Married State’?

Support your ideas with details from the text.

*A Married State*

A married state affords but little ease;
The best of husbands are so hard to please:
This in wives’ careful faces you may spell,
Though they dissemble their misfortunes well.
A virgin state is crowned with much content,
It’s always happy as it’s innocent:
No blustering husbands to create your fears,
No pangs of childbirth to extort your tears,
No children’s cries for to offend your ears,
Few worldly crosses to distract your prayers.
Thus are you freed from all the cares that do
Attend on matrimony, and a husband too.
Therefore, Madam, be advised by me:
Turn, turn apostate to love’s levity.
Suppress wild nature if she dare rebel,
There’s no such thing as leading apes in hell.

(Katherine Philips)
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In ‘A Married State’, Katherine Philips powerfully expresses her views on marriage and independence by presenting matrimony as a life filled with burdens, anxieties, and emotional restriction, in stark contrast to the freedom and happiness she associates with virginity.

From the very opening line, Philips leaves the reader in no doubt about her position: “A married state affords but little ease”. The statement is delivered as a universal truth, creating an authoritative tone that shapes the rest of the poem. The bluntness of “little ease” suggests not only discomfort, but the constant, ongoing nature of a wife’s struggles. Philips intensifies this criticism by adding that “The best of husbands are so hard to please”, implying that even an ideal husband brings dissatisfaction. The superlative “best” is ironic; it exposes how deeply embedded male authority and female obligation were in seventeenth-century expectations of marriage. Through this early tone of confident certainty, Philips frames marriage not as a romantic union, but as a trap that reduces women’s happiness and independence.

Philips reinforces this negativity through vivid emotional imagery. She invites the reader to “spell” the suffering of wives in their “careful faces”, suggesting that the strain of marriage becomes physically visible. The verb “dissemble” conveys that women must hide their unhappiness to maintain social expectations, presenting marriage as something that forces emotional suppression. This idea of performance contributes to Philips’s wider critique: not only is marriage exhausting, but it demands a constant pretence of contentment. Through this, she expresses her belief that independence is preferable to the constraints of a married life shaped by duty, expectation, and secrecy.

In contrast, Philips presents the “virgin state” as a life defined by “much content”. The phrase “always happy” creates a sense of lasting peace, while “innocent” carries both moral purity and freedom from worldly burdens. Philips uses a list-like structure to emphasise this contrast. The accumulation of negatives associated with marriage, “No blustering husbands”, “No pangs of childbirth”, “No children’s cries”, “Few worldly crosses”, highlights the sheer number of demands placed on a wife. The repetition of “No” works almost like a chant of liberation, stripping away each expectation one by one until independence appears calm, uncluttered, and enviably peaceful. This structural opposition between the two states is one of Philips’ most powerful devices in the poem.

Philips also focuses on the physical and emotional toll that marriage exacts. Childbirth “extorts” tears, a verb associated with force and violence, suggesting suffering imposed on women rather than chosen. Children’s cries “offend your ears”, implying constant disruption and the loss of personal peace. The phrase “worldly crosses” carries religious connotations of burden and sacrifice, reinforcing the idea that wives are expected to endure hardship as part of their role. In presenting these pains so starkly, Philips makes independence seem not only desirable but necessary for preserving a woman’s sense of self.

Towards the end of the poem, Philips adopts a more advisory tone as she addresses the “Madam” directly. The imperative “be advised by me” positions her as a wise counsellor, strengthening her argument through direct persuasion. The repeated “Turn, turn apostate to love’s levity” is striking: by choosing the religious word “apostate”, she suggests abandoning romantic love as though renouncing a misguided faith. Calling love “levity” reduces it to a trivial, unreliable force, far removed from the stability and dignity that Philips seems to value. This choice of language underlines her belief that emotional independence is far more beneficial to women than the uncertainty of marriage.

She ends the poem with the dismissive reassurance that unmarried women need not fear the old superstition of “leading apes in hell”, a phrase used historically to shame women who remained single. By rejecting this idea, Philips not only defends singlehood, but directly challenges patriarchal attempts to control women through fear and ridicule. The final line therefore becomes a bold declaration of independence: singleness is not a punishment but a source of freedom, unburdened by marriage’s emotional and physical strains.

Overall, Philips conveys her views on marriage and independence with a powerful, unwavering voice, using contrast, vivid imagery, and direct persuasion to present independence as a path of peace and freedom, and marriage as a life of burdens and constraint.

parts.problemMd:
In what ways does Pope clearly convey his ideas about human nature and reason in From ‘An Essay on Man’?

Support your ideas with details from the text.

*From ‘An Essay on Man’*

Know then thyself, presume not God to scan;
The proper study of mankind is man.
Placed on this isthmus of a middle state,
A being darkly wise, and rudely great:
With too much knowledge for the sceptic side,
With too much weakness for the stoic’s pride,
He hangs between; in doubt to act or rest,
In doubt to deem himself a god or beast,
In doubt his mind or body to prefer,
Born but to die, and reasoning but to err;
Alike in ignorance, his reason such,
Whether he thinks too little, or too much:
Chaos of thought and passion, all confused;
Still by himself abused or disabused;
Created half to rise and half to fall,
Great lord of all things, yet a prey to all;
Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled:
The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!

(Alexander Pope)
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In ‘An Essay on Man’, Pope offers a striking exploration of human nature and the limitations of human reason. Pope merges reason to present mankind as a “riddle”, a being trapped between extremes, and one who constantly overestimates his own wisdom.

The poem opens with a command: “Know then thyself, presume not God to scan”. By addressing the reader directly, Pope sets a moral and philosophical tone. His use of the imperative “Know” reflects the Enlightenment belief in rational self-inquiry, while “presume not God to scan” warns against human arrogance. The contrast between the achievable (understanding oneself) and the impossible (understanding God) immediately establishes Pope’s central idea: humans must accept their limits. The line also encapsulates two aspects of human nature Pope criticises: curiosity and pride. Humans want knowledge, but they aim too high.

Pope then asserts that “The proper study of mankind is man”. The repetition of the word “man” emphasises the self-contained nature of human inquiry: this is what we should understand, yet we frequently fail to do so. Pope presents humans as creatures caught in a “middle state”, poised between two extremes — ignorance and omniscience, mortality and reason. His description of humans as “A being darkly wise, and rudely great” illustrates this paradox. The oxymorons “darkly wise” and “rudely great” suggest that although humans possess flashes of intelligence, this wisdom is clouded by ignorance or roughness. The tension within these descriptions conveys Pope’s belief that human nature is contradictory.

Throughout the poem, Pope uses balanced structures. The repetition in lines “With too much knowledge for the sceptic side, / With too much weakness for the stoic’s pride” highlights how humans are ill-fitted for all extremes. Pope’s use of antithesis creates a rhythm of instability that mirrors the instability of human reason itself. Humans waver “in doubt to act or rest”, reflecting not only indecision, but also Pope’s deeper point that reason cannot fully guide us because it is itself unreliable.

Pope develops this further through a series of tight parallel structures: “In doubt to deem himself a god or beast; / In doubt his mind or body to prefer”. The balancing of “god” and “beast” conveys the arrogance and self-disgust that define different sides of human nature. Both extremes show irrational thinking — either too much pride or too much self-loathing. The pattern of “In doubt” reinforces the idea that doubt is a defining condition of humanity. Despite possessing reason, humans remain uncertain about the most fundamental questions about themselves.

The line “Born but to die, and reasoning but to err” summarises Pope’s bleak view of human limitation. The repeated structure, with “but to”, conveys inevitability: humans cannot escape mortality, and their reasoning cannot escape error. The phrase “Alike in ignorance, his reason such, / Whether he thinks too little or too much” is particularly striking. Here, Pope criticises both intellectual laziness and overthinking, suggesting that both lead to confusion. Human reason, rather than guiding us, often becomes a trap.

Pope goes on to describe humanity as a “Chaos of thought and passion, all confused”. This metaphor presents the human mind as a turbulent mixture of rationality (“thought”) and emotion (“passion”), suggesting that neither can dominate the other. The alliteration of “Chaos” and “confused” emphasises disorder. Yet, Pope also implies that this internal disorder is universal: humans are “Still by himself abused or disabused”, unable to reach stable truths. The repetition of “half” in “Created half to rise and half to fall” captures humans’ divided nature: capable of seeking improvement, yet continually dragged down by their own flaws.

The final lines convey Pope’s vision of humanity as a being of contradictions. Humans are “Great lord of all things, yet a prey to all”; this juxtaposition shows how humans exert power over their environment yet remain vulnerable to suffering, temptation, and error. The triple description — “The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!” — summarises Pope’s argument. “Glory” acknowledges human creativity; “jest” highlights human foolishness; “riddle” suggests the enigma of human nature that reason cannot fully solve. The exclamation mark ending the poem emphasises the intensity of Pope’s conclusion: humanity is fundamentally paradoxical.

In conclusion, Pope vividly conveys his ideas about human nature and the limitations of reason through direct address, balanced antithesis, and striking imagery. Humans are presented as creatures caught between extremes, capable of thought yet prone to confusion, and continually overestimating their abilities.

parts.problemMd:
How does Rumens movingly portray childhood and sacrifice in this poem?

Support your ideas with details from the text.

*Carpet-weavers, Morocco*

The children are at the loom of another world. 
Their braids are oiled and black, their dresses bright. 
Their assorted heights would make a melodious chime.

They watch their flickering knots like television. 
As the garden of Islam grows, the bench will be raised. 
Then they will lace the dark‑rose veins of the tree‑tops.

The carpet will travel in the merchant’s truck. 
It will be spread by the servants of the mosque. 
Deep and soft, it will give when heaped with prayer.

The children are hard at work in the school of days. 
From their fingers the colours of all‑that‑will‑be fly 
and freeze into the frame of all‑that‑was.

(Carol Rumens)
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In ‘Carpet-weavers, Morocco’, Rumens offers a deeply moving portrayal of childhood shaped by labour, tradition, and sacrifice. Rumens intertwines innocence with exploitation, showing how childhood dreams and colours are woven into a future that does not belong to the children themselves.

From the opening line, Rumens places the children “at the loom of another world”, establishing both the physical reality of their labour and the symbolic distance between their lives and the futures they are helping to build. The phrase “another world” implies that the beauty, luxury, and spiritual richness their carpets will bring belong elsewhere — to customers, merchants, and mosques — not to them. This immediately creates a sense of sacrifice: their creativity is devoted to purposes beyond their own childhood enjoyment. Rumens’ use of “children” foregrounds innocence, making their labour seem all the more poignant.

The poet’s description of the children’s appearance — “their braids are oiled and black, their dresses bright” — initially paints an image of colour and vibrancy. However, the brightness contrasts with the seriousness of their work, reinforcing the tension between childhood and obligation. Their “assorted heights” that “would make a melodious chime” is a gentle, lyrical image, suggesting that the children together form something harmonious and beautiful. Yet the phrase “would make” hints at a possibility rather than a reality: their potential for play and childhood unity exists only as a metaphor, not an experience. Rumens subtly suggests that their childhood “melody” is imagined rather than lived.

The comparison “They watch their flickering knots like television” introduces a modern reference that highlights how different their lives are from those of children elsewhere. Instead of passively enjoying entertainment, they focus intently on “flickering knots”, the movements of their fingers replacing the movement on a screen. The simile emphasises how childhood imagination is channelled into repetitive work. The effect is both striking and sad: labour has replaced leisure. Rumens then shifts to religious imagery — “As the garden of Islam grows, the bench will be raised” — which suggests a connection between their work and cultural tradition. As they age or gain skill, they “will lace the dark-rose veins of the tree-tops”, creating increasingly intricate patterns. The beautiful metaphor of “dark-rose veins” reinforces the artistry of their work, but it also hints at sacrifice — veins carrying lifeblood. The children pour themselves into these carpets, giving up their time, energy, and youth.

The third stanza focuses on the carpet’s journey: “The carpet will travel in the merchant’s truck. / It will be spread by the servants of the mosque.” This emphasises how the children’s work serves people and purposes far removed from their everyday lives. Rumens uses the repeated “will” to show inevitability; the carpet moves forward into the world, while the children remain behind. The description “Deep and soft, it will give when heaped with prayer” highlights the comfort the carpet provides to those who worship on it, contrasting with the discomfort and repetitiveness of the children’s labour. The tenderness of “deep and soft” reinforces the idea that the beauty they create will be appreciated by others, not by them.

The final stanza is the most poignant and reflective. Rumens writes, “The children are hard at work in the school of days”, a metaphor that replaces formal education with life’s harsher lessons. Instead of learning letters and numbers, the children learn through physical labour. The phrase suggests that childhood itself is being sacrificed as they take on responsibilities too heavy for their age. Rumens then creates a powerful image of creation and loss: “From their fingers the colours of all-that-will-be fly / and freeze into the frame of all-that-was.” This encapsulates the central theme of sacrifice. The children weave “all-that-will-be” — the future beauty, faith, and value embodied in the carpets — yet those colours “freeze” into the past. Their creative potential is captured in objects that leave them behind. The interplay of “will-be” and “was” shows how their labour becomes history while their own futures remain uncertain.

In conclusion, Rumens movingly conveys childhood and sacrifice through vivid imagery, symbolic contrasts, and the tension between beauty and labour. The children’s creativity and innocence are woven into carpets that travel far beyond them, while their own childhoods are surrendered to work and responsibility.

parts.problemMd:
How does the speaker strikingly compare his lover to summer in ‘Sonnet 18’?

Support your ideas with details from the text.

*Sonnet 18 *

Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day? 
Thou art more lovely and more temperate: 
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, 
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date: 
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines 
And often is his gold complexion dimmed; 
And every fair from fair sometime declines, 
By chance, or nature’s changing course, untrimmed. 
But thy eternal summer shall not fade, 
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st; 
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade, 
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st: 
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see, 
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

(William Shakespeare)
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In ‘Sonnet 18’, Shakespeare presents one of the most memorable and striking comparisons in English poetry, contrasting the beauty of a lover with the instability and imperfection of a summer’s day. Through vivid imagery, carefully controlled rhythm, and a tonal shift in the volta, Shakespeare conveys both admiration for the lover and awe at poetry’s ability to preserve beauty against time.

The opening question appears gentle and contemplative, yet it is also playful. The speaker already knows the answer will be “no”: the lover surpasses summer. The line “Thou art more lovely and more temperate” immediately establishes the superiority of the lover. The word “lovely” suggests physical beauty, but “temperate” suggests emotional balance and gentleness. Summer may be beautiful, but it is inconsistent; the lover, by contrast, is presented as harmonious and constant. This subtle, precise contrast sets the tone for the rest of the poem.

Shakespeare then describes summer in a way that highlights its flaws. “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May” presents a violent, almost disruptive force, with “rough winds” shaking fragile “darling buds”. The choice of “darling” emphasises tenderness, making the violence of the winds feel more striking, and showing that summer cannot protect beauty. Summer is temporary, too: “summer’s lease hath all too short a date”. This metaphor implies that its beauty is only borrowed, never permanent. The lover, however, is set up as someone who does not suffer from these natural limits.

The imperfections of summer continue in the next two lines: “Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines / And often is his gold complexion dimmed”. The “eye of heaven” metaphor for the sun elevates the image, but emphasises unpredictability — sometimes too bright, sometimes clouded, often unreliable. Shakespeare’s imagery highlights summer’s extremes: too hot, too dim, too brief. This creates a clear contrast with the lover, who is constant and even-tempered. The contrast is further strengthened by the universal truth stated in line 7: “And every fair from fair sometime declines”. Beauty fades not only because of natural causes, but also “by chance”. The word “untrimmed” emphasises the inevitability of decline.

The volta at line 9 introduces a striking shift: “But thy eternal summer shall not fade”. The lover is given an “eternal summer”, a season made permanent. The adjective “eternal” is crucial: it marks a move away from the natural world into something timeless and idealised. Shakespeare presents the lover not only as more beautiful than summer but also beyond the reach of decay. The line “Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st” uses the language of ownership to suggest that the lover’s beauty is secure, not borrowed like summer’s lease. This stability directly contrasts with earlier imagery of decline.

Shakespeare then goes further, defying death itself: “Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade”. The personification of death as boastful makes the defiance more striking. Death cannot “brag” because the lover will never be claimed by him. The idea that the lover “grow’st” into “eternal lines” underscores the power of poetry itself. It is the poem — the “eternal lines” of the sonnet — that guarantees survival. Through this bold assertion, Shakespeare shifts the comparison: the lover is not merely better than summer; they are immortalised in art.

The final couplet confirms this idea with complete confidence: “So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.” The repetition of “so long” stretches time into the distant future, and the simplicity of the phrasing reinforces its certainty. Shakespeare is not simply praising his lover; he is asserting the eternal power of poetry. As long as readers exist, the lover will continue to “live”. The comparison with summer therefore becomes symbolic: summer fades, but art endures.

In conclusion, Shakespeare compares his lover to summer only to show that the comparison ultimately fails — not because summer is imperfect, but because the lover’s beauty and constancy surpass natural boundaries. Through vivid imagery of nature’s instability, a confident and uplifting volta, and the bold celebration of poetry’s immortalising power, Shakespeare creates a comparison that is as striking as it is memorable.

parts.problemMd:
In what ways does Wright vividly convey the speaker’s awe and fear in ‘Hunting Snake’?

Support your ideas with details from the text.

*Hunting Snake*

Sun-warmed in this late season’s grace
under the autumn’s gentlest sky
we walked, and froze half-through a pace.
The great black snake went reeling by.

Head- down, tongue flickering on the trail
he quested through the parting grass;
sun glazed his curves of diamond scale,
and we lost breath to watch him pass.

What track he followed, what small food
fled living from his fierce intent,
we scarcely thought; still as we stood
our eyes went with him as he went.

Cold, dark and splendid he was gone
into the grass that hid his prey.
We took a deeper breath of day,
looked at each other, and went on.

(Judith Wright)
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In ‘Hunting Snake’, Judith Wright powerfully conveys the speaker’s mixture of awe and fear through natural imagery and a subtle shift in tone. The poem captures a brief but intense encounter with a snake, and Wright transforms this moment into a reflection on the beauty, danger, and authority of the natural world.

From the outset, Wright creates a peaceful, almost idyllic atmosphere, making the snake’s arrival all the more shocking. The opening line describes the landscape as “Sun-warmed in this late season’s grace”, a gentle and harmonious image suggesting contentment. The phrase “grace” implies a blessing or gift, conveying the speaker’s initial sense of peace within nature. This tranquillity is strengthened by “autumn’s gentlest sky”, an image of safety and warmth. The setting lulls both the speaker and the reader into a false sense of security, heightening the contrast when the snake appears. Wright’s use of a peaceful setting emphasises how awe and fear burst unexpectedly into ordinary moments.

The sudden shift in tone when the snake arrives conveys immediate fear. The poet writes that “we walked, and froze half-through a pace”, communicating a moment of shock so intense that it literally halts movement. The verb “froze” conveys both sudden stillness and instinctive fear, suggesting that the speaker’s reaction is physical and uncontrollable. The snake’s movement is described as “reeling by”, a dynamic verb that gives it a swift, unstoppable momentum. The encounter is brief but powerful, and the speaker reacts instinctively, feeling overwhelmed by the snake’s presence.

Wright presents the snake as both dangerous and majestic, creating a complex blend of awe and fear. Its “Head down, tongue flickering on the trail” conjures stereotypical images of a predator: focused, precise, and hunting. The repeated sibilance in “sun glazed his curves of diamond scale” echoes the silent movement of the snake and gives the image a shimmering quality. Calling the scales “diamond” not only suggests their shape but also gives the snake a jewel-like beauty. This combination of threat and splendour evokes admiration alongside anxiety. The speaker admits, “we lost breath to watch him pass”, a phrase that can suggest fear, awe, or a mixture of both. Their breathlessness reflects both the snake’s beauty and its capacity to cause harm.

The speaker’s awe becomes even clearer as Wright highlights the snake’s power and purpose. The creature moves with “fierce intent”, indicating a natural authority that the humans instinctively recognise. Wright expresses the speaker’s astonishment through understatement: “we scarcely thought”. In this moment, rational thought is replaced by instinctive fascination. They track the snake’s movement with their eyes, unable to look away — “our eyes went with him as he went.” This mirrored movement reinforces the speaker’s mesmerised state, and the gentle repetition of “went” suggests quiet, almost reverent observation.

When the snake finally disappears, the poem shifts to a tone of quiet reflection. The speaker describes him as “Cold, dark and splendid”, a triad of adjectives that unites fear and beauty. “Cold” and “dark” suggest danger, mystery, and inhumanity, while “splendid” conveys admiration and awe. The juxtaposition captures how the natural world can evoke contradictory emotions: fascination mixed with fear, admiration mixed with vulnerability. The snake’s disappearance “into the grass that hid his prey” restores the quiet landscape, yet it also reminds us of the ongoing cycles of life and death happening unnoticed around the speakers.

The concluding lines return to the human perspective. The speaker notes that after the snake was gone, “We took a deeper breath of day”, suggesting relief but also renewed appreciation for the world around them. Their “deeper breath” may indicate that the encounter has left them shaken, aware of how thin the line between safety and danger can be. The moment of awe has heightened their sensitivity to life itself. When they “looked at each other, and went on”, the understated ending reflects how profound experiences can be absorbed quietly, leaving a subtle but significant emotional impact.

Through this brief encounter, Wright vividly conveys awe and fear by showing how nature’s beauty and danger are intertwined. The snake is not demonised; instead, it is presented as a powerful, self-contained force deserving of respect. The speaker’s reactions — physical shock, breathless admiration, silent watching — reveal a deep emotional humility before nature’s authority. The poem ultimately celebrates the mysterious and commanding presence of the natural world.

parts.problemMd:
In what ways does Rossetti strikingly present guilt and punishment in Nick?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In Nick, Christina Rossetti strikingly presents guilt and punishment through a cyclical, cautionary tale that explores the destructive nature of envy and discontent. By employing a fairy-tale structure where the protagonist is granted the power to manifest his own malicious desires, Rossetti reveals how guilt is often suppressed by the ego, only to be forcibly experienced through self-inflicted punishment. Through vivid animalistic imagery, ironic narrative voice and the irony of failed "malice," Rossetti conveys the message that the "injury" one intends for others ultimately consumes the self.

Initially, Rossetti presents Nick’s guilt as a form of spiritual lack rather than material need. Despite having a snug house and "abundance" from his farm, he is described as "poor" because he is "discontented and envious": the blunt clause here strips Nick of excuse or complexity, presenting envy as a habitual state rather than a momentary flaw. This striking paradox sets the stage for his punishment. Nick’s guilt is not a feeling of remorse, but a moral failure that the fairy woman punishes by granting him his wishes. Punishment begins when the fairy grants Nick the power to become “everything you wish”, a strikingly ironic response that turns guilt into its own instrument of suffering. The fairy’s "slap in the face", described with the sharp simile “as if a bee had stung him”, serves as a physical catalyst for the internal change that is to follow, turning his own words into a trap. Rossetti’s choice of fairy-tale violence is deliberately mild yet humiliating, reinforcing that Nick’s punishment is corrective rather than sadistic.

The animalistic physical transformations Nick undergoes serve as a striking presentation of how malice reduces human dignity. When he wishes to be sparrows to "devastate" his neighbour’s trees, he is immediately met with the "pop, bang" of a revolver, leaving him a "crestfallen biped" with a "broken leg and wing". This is striking because it collapses predator and victim into one figure. Rossetti uses this transformation to show that acting on envy is inherently self-destructive, and the adjective “crestfallen”, associated with shame rather than pain, reinforces that punishment targets his moral pride as much as his body. This cycle intensifies when he becomes a "savage bull-dog" to kill a cat, only to find himself hunted as a "mad dog" by the entire village. The punishment is strikingly presented as a loss of identity and safety, where he is reduced to cowering in "stinging-nettles".

Rossetti’s most striking presentation of punishment occurs when Nick attempts to use his power to commit arson. As fire, he intends to "burn the cottage," but is ironically forced to contribute to the "well-being of his tormentors" by boiling their kettle and toasting their cheese. The "disagreeable conviction" that he has "caused more injury to himself than to any of his neighbours" is the true psychological punishment. The final transformation into the "rich old man" or miser is the ultimate reckoning, where the fear of being "buried alive" by his own servants provides a visceral, "unearthly" terror that finally breaks his cycle of malice.

In conclusion, Rossetti strikingly presents guilt and punishment as the inevitable harvest of an envious soul. Through the ironic failure of Nick’s transformations and the terrifying climax of his near-death experience, she shows that punishment is not just an external force but a consequence of a heart that refuses to find peace. The story ends with a reformed Nick who is "never again heard to utter a wish," suggesting that his ultimate punishment was the profound fear that finally birthed his redemption.

The response explores the imagery of the “crestfallen biped” and the “unearthly yell” in detail, showing deep engagement with how the writer uses a fairy-tale framework to deliver a harsh moral critique.

parts.problemMd:
How does Schreiner powerfully convey the narrator’s emotions and realisations in The Woman’s Rose?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In The Woman’s Rose, Olive Schreiner powerfully conveys the narrator’s transition from youthful arrogance to a realisation of female solidarity. Through the use of a retrospective narrative, Schreiner explores how a single act of grace can overcome petty competition. By contrasting the narrator’s early hunger for power with the lasting scent of a withered rose, the story reveals that true human connection is more resilient than the despair of a cynical world.

Schreiner initially establishes the narrator’s emotions through the physical setting of her memories. The narrator keeps her "trifles" in an "old, brown carved box" with a "broken" lid, suggesting that these realisations are private and perhaps fragile. She admits that when her "faith in woman grows dim," the memory of the "dead rose" returns to her as it is "in the box still". This powerfully conveys a sense of hope in female solidarity, as "spring cannot fail us" even when "love and magnanimity" can.

The narrator’s younger self is portrayed with a "vital" but "mean" emotional state. Upon arriving in a town where another woman "reigned alone," the narrator describes her own desire for dominance. She admits she was "too small to be tender" and compares herself to a "child with a new whip," which she uses to "crack" everywhere without care. This metaphor vividly conveys her reckless ego and the cynicism of her youth. Her realisation here is one of self-reflection; she looks back and sees that her "mother heart had not swelled in me yet," acknowledging that she viewed men as children to be manipulated for her pleasure.

Schreiner creates significant tension through the narrator’s "hatred" and silent rivalry with another young girl in a small town in which the population consisted "mainly of men". The narrator "hated" the other girl because she seemed "too good" to be among the worshipping men. This emotional complexity reveals a paradoxical respect hidden beneath her jealousy. Although "She and I never spoke to each other," the narrator felt the other woman’s "presence" as a weight. The realisation that the man "that had staked on me" on who was prettier at the hotel bet shows the "squalid" nature of their competition, yet the narrator remains "sure she hated me". This builds a sense of "injury" that makes the eventual act of kindness even more striking.

The climax of the story provides the most powerful emotional shift when the "fair haired girl" offers her own white rose. In the waiting-room, the girl tells the narrator, "Stand still," and fastens the rose in the narrator’s dark hair, saying it "looks much better there!". This gesture completely shatters the narrator’s expectations of petty competition. Her realisation is expressed in her simple, moved response: "You are so beautiful to me". Schreiner conveys that this moment of "love and magnanimity" is what truly matters, far more than the compliments of men. The fact that the rose is still in the box "after twelve years" proves that this realisation of female solidarity became the narrator’s most memorable truth.

In conclusion, Schreiner conveys the narrator’s emotions by moving from the bitter cold of midwinter rivalry to the radiance of a shared smile. The narrator’s journey from a "shrewd" girl with a "whip" to a woman who cherishes withered petals represents a powerful discovery of "magnanimity". Schreiner reveals that while cynicism may dim our faith, the memory of a single selfless act can ensure that "spring" will never fail.

> **Commentary**

> The essay demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the narrator’s "construct," analysing her growth from a "child with a new whip" to a woman of "faith". The response explores the imagery of the "withered rose" and the "broken box" in detail, showing deep engagement with how Schreiner uses these symbols to represent "magnanimity". Structural contrasts between the "midwinter" gardens and the "sunny corner" where the rose grows are interpreted effectively.

parts.problemMd:
How does Ellison vividly convey the narrator’s struggles and frustrations in The Black Ball?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In The Black Ball, Ralph Ellison vividly conveys the narrator’s struggles and frustrations by immersing the reader in a life governed by fear, restraint and constant vigilance. Through tightly controlled first-person narration, Ellison exposes the psychological strain of surviving as a Black working-class father in a segregated society, where dignity must be concealed beneath obedience and anger must be disguised as “industry”. The narrator’s frustration arises not from a single injustice, but from the relentless awareness that a single mistake, a “black ball”, could erase his fragile security.

Ellison first conveys this struggle through the narrator’s relationship with his work. The meticulous description of “mopping the lobby” and “polishing the brass” is infused with an exaggerated sense of care, revealing how labour becomes a form of self-preservation. The narrator’s repeated focus on the “luster” of the brass exposes his anxiety, as Berry judges his value not by his humanity, but by reflective surfaces. When the narrator observes that, for Berry, “I was there” only alongside “his money” and “plants”, Ellison uses blunt, declarative syntax to emphasise the narrator’s erasure. The chilling simplicity of the phrase reduces the man to an object, reinforcing the narrator’s awareness that his existence is conditional and replaceable. His fear of being labelled a “damned educated” man further exposes his frustration, as intelligence itself becomes a liability in a system designed to suppress ambition.

The narrator’s frustration deepens most painfully in his role as a father, where Ellison exposes the emotional cost of survival. When his four-year-old son asks, “Daddy, am I black?”, the narrator’s response, “you’re brown”, reveals a linguistic evasion shaped by fear. Ellison’s use of dialogue here is deceptively simple, mirroring the child’s innocence while highlighting the father’s moral conflict. The narrator’s need to lie underscores the cruelty of a society that forces parents to protect their children through distortion rather than truth. This tension escalates when the boy is tricked into handing over his ball. The visual contrast between the child’s “tears on his face” and Berry “red in the face” with rage reinforces the power imbalance; the narrator knows his son is innocent, but is powerless to argue. All he can do is give Berry "one long hard look" and do as he is asked.

Ellison broadens the narrator’s struggle through the encounter with the union man, using physical imagery to embody social violence. The man’s “scarred” and “fried hands” function as a visceral reminder of the brutality underpinning racial hierarchies. Initially, the narrator’s instinctive hostility, his urge to “choke” the man, reflects his fear of disruption rather than ideological opposition. However, when he studies the “skin drawn and puckered”, Ellison slows the narrative pace, forcing both narrator and reader into a moment of recognition. The tactile imagery transforms abstract injustice into bodily suffering, unsettling the narrator’s assumptions.

By the end of the story, Ellison crystallises the narrator’s struggle through the metaphor of the “black ball”, a symbol of exclusion that governs both social systems and childhood games. The narrator’s reflection that his son is already “learning the rules of the game” reveals the tragic inheritance of frustration, passed from parent to child. The final image of the narrator touching the union card while thinking of the “fried hands” unites physical pain, moral awakening and unresolved fear. Ellison thus conveys struggle not through dramatic confrontation, but through the suffocating discipline of restraint, where survival itself becomes a form of resistance.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is a 25-mark question. This answer would be securely placed in Level 8, as it shows a perceptive, detailed, and well-supported understanding of how Ellison conveys the narrator's psychological and social struggles.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The essay demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the narrator’s construct, analysing how his "industry" is a survival mechanism in a segregated USA. The response explores Ellison’s imagery in detail, such as the "fried hands" and the "black ball" as a symbol of exclusion, showing deep engagement with how language reveals "frustration". Structural contrasts between the domestic scenes with the son and the tense exchanges with Berry are interpreted effectively.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - **Analyse** how the narrator’s **invisible status** in Berry’s office is a **striking metaphor** for the wider **racial hierarchy** of the 1930s
> - **Explore** how the fried hands of the union man serve as a **harrowing visual reminder** of the **conqueror’s face** in history
> - **Discuss** the irony of the son’s white ball being thrown by a white boy, showing how the narrator must **teach the rules** of a **rigged game**

parts.problemMd:
In what ways does Anand vividly portray the narrator’s pride and disillusionment in The Gold Watch?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In The Gold Watch, Mulk Raj Anand vividly portrays Srijut Sharma’s journey from "deep obsessive fear" to a state of total emotional disillusionment. By using the gold watch as a central ironic symbol, Anand explores the "bitter pill" of forced retirement in a marketised colonial workplace, where long-term loyalty is met with cold indifference.

Anand initially conveys Sharma’s disillusionment through the predatory presentation of his employer, Mr Acton. Even when Acton offers a smile, Sharma recognises it as an ominous sign. The repetition of "smile" emphasises this sense of unease, as Mr Acton was "not known to smile too much". The writer creates a sense of dread by describing the boss’ "tobacco-stained" teeth and a "snarl" that is barely suppressed. This physical detail vividly suggests that for a clerk like Sharma, there is no real pride to be found in being "singled out" by the "Sahib". Instead, Sharma’s reaction is purely physical and fearful; the "sweat sozzled" his body as he realises his "doom was sealed". This portrays disillusionment as a life-altering shock.

The element of pride in the story is shown to be a fragile façade that Sharma maintains for his family. During the weekend, he performs an "exaggerated bonhomie" to hide his "panic and confusion" from his wife and son. His disillusionment is most painful when he gives his old silver watch to his son, Hari. While the boy "capered" with joy, Sharma knows the new gold watch is merely a token used to "sugarcoat" his dismissal five years before it should have been. By showing Sharma as an "accomplished natural actor," Anand emphasizes that his pride is not a position of strength, but a desperate attempt to maintain his "nobility of soul" while facing financial ruin.

The final portrayal of disillusionment occurs when Sharma receives the gift in an "abject manner". Anand uses the metaphor of a "beggar receiving alms" to show the total loss of Sharma’s professional dignity. The "beautiful red case" of the watch is a hollow distraction from the "fumes of frustration" Sharma feels but cannot voice. The ultimate disillusionment is captured in the fact that the watch "only went when it was shaken". This symbolic detail mirrors Sharma’s own life; after twenty years of "clock-work efficiency," he is left with a broken machine and "involuntary tears".

In conclusion, Anand portrays disillusionment as the inevitable result of a system that views humans as replaceable parts. Through the contrast of the gold symbol and Sharma’s humiliation, the writer vividly conveys how the "privilege" of the gift is actually the instrument of his destruction.

The response explores Anand’s imagery in detail, such as the predatory "tobacco-stained" teeth of Acton and the "sweat sozzled" body of the protagonist, showing deep engagement with how language reveals the visceral nature of "humiliation".

parts.problemMd:
In what ways does Atwood vividly portray the narrator’s anxieties and state of mind in When It Happens?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In When It Happens, Margaret Atwood vividly portrays Mrs Burridge’s anxieties and state of mind by depicting a middle-aged woman caught between a "daily routine of household chores" and the "frightening reality" of an impending disaster. Through a shifting narrative that blurs the line between present preparation and future survival, Atwood explores the psychological strain of a character who feels beleaguered and isolated in a world that has lost its "unquestionable belief" in stability.

Atwood initially conveys Mrs Burridge’s anxiety through her obsessive focus on preservation. The act of "putting up green tomato pickles" is described as a race against a "killer frost," suggesting that her state of mind is dominated by a need to outrun a perceived "doom". The pickles are more than food; they represent her fragile security. Her anxiety is vividly captured when she carries the jars down the cellar stairs, a place that used to make her feel safe but now triggers a "peculiar thought". She worries that she won't be able to "take any of the jars with her" because they are "too heavy to carry," revealing a mind already living in a state of "forced migration" even before the disaster has arrived.

Her state of mind is further revealed through her loss of faith in the future. Atwood portrays Mrs Burridge as someone who can no longer "believe in a distant future that is orderly like the past". Her traditional list-making, once a symbol of "industry," becomes a harrowing symptom of her disoriented state. While she writes "Oatmeal" or "Cheese" on her calendar, she is simultaneously imagining "columns of smoke" and the "black and oily" aftermath of an explosion. This binary opposition between her "evenly spaced public-school handwriting" and her vision of a "sticky puddle that looks like blood" vividly conveys a mind that is "fractured" by fear.

Finally, Atwood portrays Mrs Burridge’s anxiety through her physical and social vulnerability. She looks at her husband, Frank, and realises he "can't protect me" because he walks "slower than he used to". This realisation that the "men have lost the power" creates an "air of helplessness" that exasperates her. Her decision to hide the shotgun under roofing behind the barn without telling Frank shows a shrewd and secretive survival instinct. By the end of the story, her anxiety has transformed into a "fatalism" where her "hands feel thick and wooden" as she prepares for a violent encounter, showing that she has already surrendered her innocence to the "rules of the game".

The response explores Atwood’s imagery in detail, such as the "cellar jars" and the "sticky puddle," showing deep engagement with how language reveals a "conflicted identity." parts.problemMd:
How does Ballard vividly convey the narrator’s fascination and unease in The Man Who Walked on the Moon?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

Ballard vividly conveys the narrator’s fascination with Scranton while simultaneously creating a persistent sense of unease by presenting the “man who walked on the moon” as both extraordinary and disturbingly ordinary. This tension is rooted in the narrator’s own emotional emptiness, which makes Scranton’s fantasy alluring but also deeply unsettling.

From their first encounter, the narrator is drawn to Scranton through imagery that elevates him above the mundane world of Copacabana. Although Scranton appears physically degraded, with his “threadbare tropical suit” and “hangdog gaze”, Ballard describes him as if he exists in a different dimension. He repeatedly gazes “across the street at the vistas of an invisible space”, a phrase which immediately blurs the boundary between reality and imagination. The narrator is fascinated because Scranton seems to see beyond the noisy, commercial city, and this aligns with the narrator’s own longing to escape his failed career and oppressive domestic life. Ballard reinforces this fascination by making the city appear trivial and claustrophobic, full of “pickpockets”, “lottery tickets” and “cheap scent”, while Scranton is associated with silence, emptiness and distance.

However, Ballard ensures that this fascination is never comfortable. Unease seeps into the narrative through the physical decay of Scranton’s surroundings. His room behind the Luxor Cinema is described in grotesque detail, with “sweat” and “mucus-stained” newspapers, creating an almost diseased atmosphere. The narrator’s disappointment when the photographs turn out to be merely magazine cuttings highlights his growing fear that Scranton’s fantasy is hollow. Yet paradoxically, this realisation does not destroy the narrator’s fascination. Instead, Ballard makes the unease deeper by showing that Scranton’s belief is sincere. There is “not the slightest doubt that Scranton was sincere”, which forces the narrator, and the reader, to question whether emotional truth matters more than factual truth.

Ballard also conveys unease by drawing unsettling parallels between Scranton and the narrator himself. As the narrator becomes increasingly involved with Scranton, the world begins to lose solidity. Pedestrians become “shadow players” and the city seems to part like a "lunar landscape”. This imagery suggests psychological detachment and hints at the narrator’s own slide into illusion. His fascination is therefore self-destructive, as Scranton’s vision offers relief from reality but erodes his grip on it. The final revelation, when the narrator calmly claims “Yes, I am the astronaut”, confirms that the unease has fully taken over. Fascination has turned into identification, and admiration into imitation.

Ultimately, Ballard conveys fascination and unease by making Scranton’s moon-walking both a lie and a truth. The narrator is drawn to Scranton because he embodies a purer, lonelier vision of existence, stripped of social expectations. At the same time, this vision is terrifying because it requires the abandonment of reality itself. Ballard’s subtle use of imagery, contrast and narrative voice ensures that the narrator’s fascination feels inevitable, while the unease lingers long after the story ends.

The response explores Ballard's imagery in detail, such as the "mucus stained" newspapers showing deep engagement with how language reveals humiliation and unease. Quotations are precise, well-chosen and well-embedded, and the argument remains coherent and insightful throughout. This is a confident, perceptive Level 8 response.

parts.problemMd:
Explore the ways in which Kincaid portrays memory and self-discovery in A Walk to the Jetty.

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In A Walk to the Jetty, Kincaid presents memory as both an emotional archive and a means through which the narrator comes to understand herself at the moment of irreversible change. The walk to the jetty becomes a symbolic journey in which remembered experiences surface involuntarily, shaping Annie John’s painful but necessary self-discovery as she prepares to leave Antigua forever.

From the opening, memory is shown to be intrusive and overwhelming rather than comforting. Annie wakes with her own name filling her mind, repeated and insistent, suggesting an urgent attempt to define herself independently of her parents and her home. This fixation on her name reflects a moment of self-recognition, as if she must assert her identity before it is reshaped by departure. Kincaid reinforces this by filling Annie’s room with remembered objects: school prizes, shells from the sea, books and clothes. These items act as physical anchors to her past, each triggering reflection, yet they also emphasise how completely her identity has been constructed within this space. The room is described as entirely known to her, “inside out and outside in”, conveying how memory offers certainty even as she is forced to abandon it.

As Annie leaves the house, memory becomes increasingly fragmented and fluid, mirroring her emotional disorientation. During the walk, places from different stages of her life appear in rapid succession, often without clear transitions. Kincaid’s long, flowing sentences replicate the uncontrollable rush of recollection, suggesting that memory does not follow logic but emotional significance. Annie recalls childhood independence, such as her first solo walk to the chemist, moments of pride when her mother praised her, and incidents of humiliation, like her apprenticeship with Miss Dulcie. These memories reveal Annie’s growing awareness that her past contains both affection and cruelty, helping her to recognise that separation is not simply loss but also release.

Crucially, memory exposes the central tension in Annie’s self-discovery: her conflicted relationship with her mother. Early memories emphasise intimacy and admiration, such as sharing scents, routines and public praise. However, later recollections reveal control and hypocrisy, particularly Annie’s anger at her mother’s insistence on separation while claiming devotion. Annie’s reflection that “it is I who have changed” shows a moment of mature self-awareness. Rather than idealising the past, she recognises her emotional growth and accepts that she no longer fits comfortably within her childhood identity.

At the jetty itself, memory shifts from reflection to fear. Annie recalls earlier visits with her father, where the jetty was associated with danger and incomprehension. This resurfaces as visceral panic, linking childhood vulnerability with her present uncertainty. The repeated phrase “I shall never see this again” encapsulates how memory intensifies loss by projecting it into the future. Yet this painful awareness is also central to self-discovery, as Annie realises she must endure this knowledge rather than retreat from it.

By the final farewell, memory no longer overwhelms Annie but sharpens her resolve. Although she clings to her parents’ hands, she reminds herself that she is not a "child anymore”, marking a decisive moment of self-definition. The image of her mother shrinking into a dot on the sea symbolises how memory will persist, but at a distance, allowing Annie to move forward.

Overall, Kincaid portrays memory as a force that both wounds and clarifies. Through vivid sensory detail, fragmented structure and reflective narration, she shows that Annie’s self-discovery emerges not from rejecting her past, but from confronting it fully at the moment of departure.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is a 25-mark question. This answer would be securely placed in Level 8 as it shows a perceptive, detailed and well-supported understanding of the ways in which Kincaid portrays memory and self-discovery in A Walk to the Jetty.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> This essay demonstrates a sophisticated ability to use details, such as the repetition of Annie's name, the objects in the room, the jetty memories with her father and the final image of her mother to support the argument about memory and self-discovery. It argues conceptual ideas, demonstrating independent critical thinking, and analysis is woven into every paragraph. The response maintains one controlling argument from start to finish.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - **Do not just list** memories; **show** how memories **surface**, **interrupt** and **overwhelm** Annie
> - **Explore** how Annie’s **self-discovery** comes from **recognising change**, not simply from **leaving**
> - **Use** the **jetty** as a **psychological space**, not just a setting, as this is where **memory**, **fear** and **identity** collide

parts.problemMd:
How does Gardam powerfully convey the boy’s experiences and emotions in Showing the Flag?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

Jane Gardam powerfully conveys the boy’s experiences and emotions in Showing the Flag by closely aligning the narration with Philip’s thoughts and perceptions, allowing the reader to inhabit his fear, loneliness and gradual emotional awakening. Through vivid physical detail, symbolic objects such as the Union Jack, and shifts between external observation and intense interior monologue, Gardam presents Philip’s journey as both a physical crossing and an emotional ordeal.

From the opening, Gardam establishes Philip’s vulnerability through physical description and action. He is introduced as “the boy with big ears”, immediately marking him as exposed and childlike, while the detail that his father “was dead” places him in a position of emotional fragility. His effortful movement up the gangplank, “heaved up his two immense suitcases”, conveys not only the literal weight he carries but the emotional burden of travelling alone. Gardam reinforces his isolation by contrasting Philip’s silent endurance with the adults’ conversation about him, which he cannot hear but which reduces him to an object of discussion. The phrase “we teach our children how to endure” is bitterly ironic, as Philip’s endurance is shown to be enforced rather than chosen.

Gardam powerfully captures Philip’s inner life through free indirect discourse, allowing his thoughts to flow without clear separation from the narration. His observations of the seagulls, for example, initially appear innocent, yet quickly reveal his anxiety about foreignness and belonging. He wonders whether they are “French or English seagulls” and concludes they are “ahead of people”, because they do not need to “learn French”. This thought is poignant and revealing: Philip’s fear of language barriers and exclusion is projected onto the birds, showing how deeply his apprehension about France troubles him. Gardam uses this moment to underline his childish logic and emotional confusion, making his fear both understandable and moving.

The Union Jack functions as the central symbol through which Gardam explores Philip’s emotional state. Initially, the flag represents safety, order and his mother’s controlling presence, as he repeatedly checks the “small brass tin” to reassure himself it is still there. When the flag blows away “among the seagulls” and disappears into the “churning sea”, the moment is charged with emotional shock. Gardam slows the description, tracing the flag’s movement “up and down” until it becomes “a little bright speck”, mirroring Philip’s sense of losing his last connection to home. This loss intensifies his panic and sense of abandonment, particularly as he enters France without the symbol that was meant to guarantee his recognition and protection.

As Philip arrives in France, Gardam conveys his emotional overwhelm through fragmented sentences and bleak imagery. The repeated refrain “No Union Jack” becomes a rhythmic expression of his fear and anger, while the landscape is described in dull, regulated terms: “Rain. Fields. Grey. Everything measured out by rulers.” This stripped-back style reflects Philip’s numbness and emotional rigidity, as he tries to impose order on a world that feels hostile and incomprehensible. His growing resentment towards his mother is expressed through increasingly extreme and paranoid thoughts, culminating in the shocking belief that she “wanted him lost”. Gardam does not soften these thoughts; instead, she presents them directly, allowing the reader to experience the raw intensity of a child’s anger and grief when he feels unloved.

However, Gardam also shows Philip’s emotional resilience. Despite his fear, he physically defends his suitcases against the ruffians, acting with “a vehemence that astonished” everyone, including himself. This moment marks a subtle shift in his self-perception: he is no longer merely enduring but actively resisting. Gardam conveys this through dynamic verbs such as “flung” and “cried out”, which contrast with his earlier passive suffering and suggest a growing sense of agency.

The ending powerfully resolves Philip’s emotional journey. After convincing himself that his mother does not love him, the discovery of her note, “Oh Philip, my darling… I do so love you”, abruptly undercuts his anger and despair. The final image of the “spare Union Jack” pinned to the letter transforms the flag’s symbolism: it no longer represents rigid control or national identity but reassurance and care. Gardam’s restraint here is crucial; she avoids sentimentality, allowing the simple gesture to carry emotional weight. The delayed revelation makes the ending all the more powerful, as it exposes how easily Philip’s fear led him to misinterpret love as rejection.

Overall, Gardam conveys Philip’s experiences and emotions with striking power by immersing the reader in his inner world and using symbolism, imagery and narrative voice to reflect his shifting emotional state. The story is compelling because it does not diminish the intensity of a child’s feelings, treating Philip’s fear, anger and relief as profoundly real. This sensitive and controlled portrayal ensures the reader fully shares his journey from abandonment to understanding.

parts.problemMd:
In what ways does Forna movingly explore love and memory in Haywards Heath?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In Haywards Heath, Aminatta Forna movingly explores love and memory by presenting love as something enduring yet vulnerable to time, and memory as both sustaining and destructive. Through Attila’s reflective journey, Forna shows how memory preserves intimacy even as reality erodes it, creating a quiet but devastating emotional tension between what was and what can no longer be reclaimed.

From the outset, Forna frames the story through Attila’s consciousness, allowing memory to shape his experience of the present. His journey is meticulously planned, yet emotionally driven, suggesting that memory operates beneath rational control. Although he appears calm, his physical reactions betray suppressed emotion: his heart “beat wildly” and his scalp “tightened in alarm”. This physical response shows that Rosie remains deeply embedded in him, even after decades apart. Forna makes love feel involuntary and persistent, something that resurfaces despite time, distance and logic.

Memory is often triggered by place, and Forna uses Haywards Heath itself as a symbolic landscape of the past. The town name, once a private joke between Attila and Rosie, instantly pulls him back into shared intimacy. His recollection of her teasing overseas students about its pronunciation shows how memory preserves not grand moments but small, personal details. These remembered gestures are tender and precise, conveying a love rooted in familiarity and shared humour rather than sentimentality.

When Attila finally sees Rosie, Forna heightens the emotional impact by focusing on restraint and silence rather than overt declaration. Their conversation is fragmented and understated, and the line “They sat in silence and the silence felt comfortable already” suggests that their bond still exists without words. This moment is deeply moving because it implies that love survives even when language fails. Forna avoids melodrama, instead allowing emotional weight to build through pauses and what remains unsaid.

However, memory is also shown as painful and destabilising. Attila’s regret surfaces when he recalls leaving Rosie for his scholarship, asking himself “Which one of them had been naïve?” The rhetorical question exposes his lingering guilt and self-reproach. Love here is inseparable from loss; memory forces Attila to confront the consequences of his past choices. Forna presents memory as something that cannot be controlled or edited, only endured.

The most moving exploration of love and memory occurs when Rosie begins to forget Attila. Her gentle confusion, asking him to repeat his name and later mistaking him for someone else, is devastating precisely because it is delivered without cruelty or drama. When she says, “I’m afraid you’ll have to tell me your name again, dear,” Forna shows how memory’s erosion threatens love’s survival. Yet Rosie’s warmth remains unchanged, suggesting that love can persist even when its object is no longer fully remembered.

The final scene crystallises Forna’s exploration of love with painful clarity. Rosie dances with the young carer while Attila watches silently, recognising that her happiness now exists independently of him. The repetition of Rosie’s earlier phrase, “Another turn, Attila?”, now addressed to someone else, emphasises the passage of time and Attila’s displacement. Yet the young man’s response, “Whatever makes you happy, Rosie” mirrors Attila’s own selfless love. In this moment, love becomes an act of letting go. Attila’s decision to sit down and watch, rather than intervene, demonstrates a mature, compassionate love that prioritises Rosie’s present joy over his own longing.

Overall, Forna movingly explores love and memory by showing love as enduring but not possessive, and memory as fragile yet powerful. Through quiet scenes, restrained dialogue and a deeply reflective narrative voice, the story captures the ache of remembering someone who can no longer fully remember you. The emotional power lies in Forna’s refusal to resolve this tension neatly, leaving the reader with a profound sense of love’s persistence in the face of inevitable loss.

parts.problemMd:
How does Gunesekera strikingly portray deception and misunderstanding in Fluke?

Support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In Fluke, Romesh Gunesekera strikingly portrays deception and misunderstanding through irony, layered narration and the contrast between appearance and reality. By filtering events through the calm, observant voice of the driver-narrator, Gunesekera exposes how deception is normalised and even celebrated, while misunderstanding becomes a comfortable state people choose rather than challenge.

From the opening, deception is embedded in surfaces and performance. Mr Weerakoon’s appearance is meticulously described: his tight blue suit, matching briefcase and “smart silvery laptop” all signal modern success and expertise. However, the narrator subtly undercuts this image by noting the case is made of “pretend leather”, immediately suggesting artificiality beneath the polished exterior. This early detail establishes a key theme: Weerakoon’s authority rests on image rather than substance, and those around him accept this deception because it reassures them.

Misunderstanding is reinforced through language, particularly business jargon. Weerakoon’s presentation is full of “bullet points”, “bell curves” and “market segmentation”, which the narrator admits sounds like “hot air”. Despite this, the audience appears impressed. Gunesekera uses this gap between meaning and reception to show how misunderstanding thrives when people are unwilling to admit confusion. The narrator’s honest admission that he cannot fully follow the presentation contrasts with the delegates’ silent compliance, highlighting how deception relies on collective pretence.

The narrator himself becomes complicit in deception, though in a quieter, more troubling way. His claim to have a “knack with machines” borders on superstition, involving magnetism and “good chi”, yet it successfully fixes the projector. This moment is striking because it blurs the line between genuine skill and coincidence. Weerakoon’s enthusiastic response, “Bravo! How did you do that?”, shows how easily success is mythologised. Gunesekera suggests that misunderstanding often begins with chance, then hardens into belief once it proves useful.

National and political deception is explored through casual conversation rather than dramatic exposition. The discussion of the navy’s shift from war to whale-watching tourism reveals how violent histories are repackaged as commercial opportunity. Weerakoon’s language is disturbingly flippant, treating war, tourism and profit as interchangeable strategies. His references to Pearl Harbor and military “lessons” expose a mindset that disguises aggression as strategic thinking. The narrator’s discomfort, expressed through his silence and eventual withdrawal, shows an awareness that such deception depends on forgetting inconvenient truths.

The most striking portrayal of misunderstanding comes at the end, when Weerakoon panics over his missing phone. The device, supposedly essential and secure, is found easily in the van, its PIN still the “usual four zeros”. This detail is quietly damning. It reveals that the man who sells “Marketing: The Secret of Success” cannot even protect his own information. The misunderstanding here is profound: Weerakoon believes he is in control, yet everything about him suggests carelessness masked as confidence. The narrator’s reflection that “Marketing is a doddle. Dealing with a cock-up is the real problem” delivers the story’s central insight with understated force.

The final image of “sleep” and “amnesia” broadens deception into a human condition. Gunesekera suggests that people actively choose misunderstanding because it allows them to live comfortably with past mistakes, moral compromises and unresolved guilt. The narrator’s awareness of this temptation, and his recognition of how easily one can “float on our great comfortable sea of amnesia”, gives the ending its unsettling power.

Overall, Gunesekera portrays deception and misunderstanding as systemic rather than exceptional. Through irony, symbolic detail and a restrained narrative voice, *Fluke* exposes a world where appearances replace truth and misunderstanding becomes a form of survival. The story is striking because it does not condemn outright; instead, it quietly reveals how willingly people deceive themselves, and how easily others collude in that deception.

The commentary on the "fluke" of the projector is particularly strong, and by exploring the narrator's use of "magnestism" and "good chi" to fix the machine captures the ludicrous reality that Weerakoon's success is built on chance rather than the secret of success he claims to sell.
