parts.problemMd:
Read this passage from the short story ‘The Woman’s Rose’, and then answer the question that follows it. The narrator, a girl of fifteen, is spending her last evening in a small town where she and another young woman have been rivals for the attention of the men. Here she arrives at a party given in her honour.

It was midwinter. There was nothing in the gardens but a few dahlias and chrysanthemums, and I suppose that for two hundred miles round there was not a rose to be bought for love or money. Only in the garden of a friend of mine, in a sunny corner between the oven and the brick wall, there was a rose tree growing which had on it one bud. It was white, and it had been promised to the fair haired girl to wear at the party.

** **

The evening came; when I arrived and went to the waiting-room, to take off my mantle, I found the girl there already. She was dressed in pure white, with her great white arms and shoulders showing, and her bright hair glittering in the candle-light, and the white rose fastened at her breast. She looked like a queen. I said “Good-evening,” and turned away quickly to the glass to arrange my old black scarf across my old black dress.

** **

Then I felt a hand touch my hair.

** **

“Stand still,” she said.

** **

I looked in the glass. She had taken the white rose from her breast, and was fastening it in my hair.

** **

“How nice dark hair is; it sets off flowers so.” She stepped back and looked at me. “It looks much better there!”

** **

I turned round.

** **

“You are so beautiful to me,” I said.

** **

“Y-e-s,” she said, with her slow Colonial drawl; “I’m so glad.”

** **

We stood looking at each other.

** **

Then they came in and swept us away to dance. All the evening we did not come near to each other. Only once, as she passed, she smiled at me.

** **

The next morning I left the town.

** **

I never saw her again.

How does Schreiner make this such a moving and surprising moment in the story?

Remember to support your ideas with details from the writing.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In this passage, Schreiner turns what we expect to be a moment of rivalry into a moment of real kindness, and I found it very moving because the gift comes from the person the narrator thought hated her.

At the start of the passage Schreiner builds up how alone and plain the narrator feels next to her rival. It is “midwinter” and there is “not a rose to be bought for love or money”, which makes the single white rose feel rare and precious before we even know what will happen to it. When the narrator sees the other girl “dressed in pure white” with “the white rose fastened at her breast”, she says “She looked like a queen.” The simile shows how the narrator still sees the other girl as above her, and the contrast with her own “old black scarf” and “old black dress” makes her feel small and vulnerable, even though earlier in the story the men all preferred her. I think the repeated word “old” matters here, because it shows how little confidence she has in this moment.

The turning point is sudden and quiet. Schreiner writes “Then I felt a hand touch my hair”, and putting this on its own line makes us pause, just as the narrator does. The short command “Stand still” is surprising, because we expect the rival to be cruel, and instead she takes “the white rose from her breast” and fastens it in the narrator’s hair. That white rose has been a motif for the other girl’s beauty, so giving it away is a real act of generosity. Her line “How nice dark hair is; it sets off flowers so” is kind and completely changes the feeling of the scene from competition to warmth.

What makes it most moving for me is how little needs to be said. The narrator can only manage “You are so beautiful to me”, and the other girl’s slow reply, “Y-e-s... I’m so glad”, with the drawl stretched out, feels honest and unshowy. Then Schreiner writes “We stood looking at each other”, a simple line that holds all the understanding that has passed between them without either of them explaining it. After a whole story of silence and rivalry, this quiet look means more than any speech.

The ending of the passage is deliberately plain and a little sad. “The next morning I left the town. I never saw her again.” The short, flat sentences show that this one moment was all they had, which makes it feel even more precious. Because the first-person narrative has already told us that the narrator keeps the rose in a box years later, we understand that this small act of kindness stayed with her for life.

Overall, Schreiner makes this moment moving and surprising by setting up rivalry and then breaking it with a single generous gesture. Through the contrast of the white rose against the black dress, the quiet dialogue and the flat, final sentences, she shows how one act of kindness between two women can matter more than all the attention of the men around them.

> 
> The response stays anchored in the printed extract, working through it in order: the midwinter setting and the rarity of the rose, the “queen”-like rival against the narrator’s “old black dress”, the quiet turn at “Then I felt a hand touch my hair”, the understated dialogue, and the flat closing sentences. Each point names a method — the simile, the contrast, the rose motif, the short sentences — and explains its effect on the reader, while the personal response (“I found it very moving”, “for me”) is genuine and evaluative. parts.problemMd:
Read this passage from the opening of the short story ‘Nick’, and then answer the question that follows it.

There dwelt in a small village, not a thousand miles from Fairyland, a poor man, who had no family to labour for or friend to assist. When I call him poor, you must not suppose he was a homeless wanderer, trusting to charity for a night’s lodging; on the contrary, his stone house, with its green verandah and flower-garden, was the prettiest and snuggest in all the place, the doctor’s only excepted. Neither was his store of provisions running low: his farm supplied him with milk, eggs, mutton, butter, poultry, and cheese in abundance; his fields with hops and barley for beer, and wheat for bread; his orchard with fruit and cider; and his kitchen-garden with vegetables and wholesome herbs. He had, moreover, health, an appetite to enjoy all these good things, and strength to walk about his possessions. No, I call him poor because, with all these, he was discontented and envious. It was in vain that his apples were the largest for miles around, if his neighbour’s vines were the most productive by a single bunch; it was in vain that his lambs were fat and thriving, if some one else’s sheep bore twins: so, instead of enjoying his own prosperity, and being glad when his neighbours prospered too, he would sit grumbling and bemoaning himself as if every other man’s riches were his poverty. And thus it was that one day our friend Nick leaned over Giles Hodge’s gate, counting his cherries.

** **

‘Yes,’ he muttered, ‘I wish I were sparrows to eat them up, or a blight to kill your fine trees altogether.’

** **

The words were scarcely uttered when he felt a tap on his shoulder, and looking round, perceived a little rosy woman, no bigger than a butterfly, who held her tiny fist clenched in a menacing attitude. She looked scornfully at him, and said: ‘Now listen, you churl, you! henceforward you shall straightway become everything you wish; only mind, you must remain under one form for at least an hour.’ Then she gave him a slap in the face, which made his cheek tingle as if a bee had stung him, and disappeared with just so much sound as a dewdrop makes in falling.

How does Rossetti vividly introduce the character of Nick in this passage?

Remember to support your ideas with details from the writing.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In the opening of ‘Nick’, Rossetti introduces her main character as a man who has everything he could want but is still miserable because of his envy, and she does it in a light, fairy-tale way that makes his fault clear and even a little funny.

Rossetti begins by playing with the word “poor”. She calls Nick “a poor man”, but then spends a whole paragraph listing everything he owns: his “stone house, with its green verandah and flower-garden”, and a farm that gives him “milk, eggs, mutton, butter, poultry, and cheese in abundance”. This long list of good things makes us expect a happy man, so when she explains that he is only “poor” because he is “discontented and envious”, the word is turned on its head. I think this is a clever way to introduce him, because it tells us straight away that his real poverty is inside him, not in his circumstances.

Rossetti then shows exactly how his envy works. She writes that “it was in vain that his apples were the largest for miles around, if his neighbour’s vines were the most productive by a single bunch.” The small detail of “a single bunch” is important, because it shows that even the tiniest advantage in someone else ruins all his own success. The narrative voice here feels gently mocking, especially in the line that he sat “grumbling and bemoaning himself as if every other man’s riches were his poverty.” By comparing other people’s wealth to his own “poverty”, Rossetti makes his envy sound both childish and a bit ridiculous, which sets up the comic tone of the story.

The protagonist is brought to life through his own words. Leaning over “Giles Hodge’s gate, counting his cherries”, Nick mutters, “I wish I were sparrows to eat them up, or a blight to kill your fine trees altogether.” Letting us hear him speak makes his spite feel real and personal, and the wish to become a “blight” shows how far his envy goes, because he would rather destroy good things than let anyone else enjoy them. This wish, spoken in the first person, also matters because, as readers soon learn, his wishes are about to come true.

Finally, Rossetti introduces the fairy-tale danger that will punish him. The “little rosy woman, no bigger than a butterfly” appears with her “fist clenched”, and her curse that he “shall straightway become everything you wish” is the turning point of the whole story. Even here the narrative tone stays light: the slap that makes “his cheek tingle as if a bee had stung him”, and her leaving “with just so much sound as a dewdrop makes in falling”, are gentle, delicate images which keep the story feeling like a fable rather than something frightening.

Overall, Rossetti vividly introduces Nick as a comic but flawed character whose envy is his real problem. Through the twist on the word “poor”, the mocking narrative voice, his own spiteful wish and the arrival of the fairy, she makes us understand his fault clearly and prepares us for the punishment that is coming.

parts.problemMd:
Explore the ways in which Wells strikingly depicts how the Martians invade Earth.

Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In The War of the Worlds, H. G. Wells strikingly depicts the Martian invasion of Earth as sudden, terrifying and unstoppable. Instead of presenting a fair fight or a heroic war, Wells shows humanity as helpless against a force with superior technology and inhuman detachment. Through the novel’s first-person form, its escalating structure and its vivid, unsettling language, Wells makes the invasion feel both physically destructive and psychologically overwhelming.

Wells structures the invasion so that it begins with curiosity rather than immediate horror. The strange arrival from space draws crowds who treat it like a spectacle, which creates dramatic irony because the reader quickly senses danger. This slow build makes the invasion more striking because it shows how unprepared humans are. Wells delays the full appearance of violence, allowing tension to rise as the cylinder is observed and its movement described in controlled, mechanical detail. The careful pacing makes the later chaos feel sudden and brutal, as the reader experiences the moment when ordinary life collapses.

Wells’ language also makes the Martians frightening because they are presented as unnatural and unfamiliar. He avoids describing them in ways that would make them seem human-like, instead emphasising their alien physicality and strange presence. This unfamiliarity creates fear because the narrator, and the reader, cannot rely on normal expectations. Wells often focuses on unsettling details and odd movement, suggesting something grotesque and difficult to comprehend. The invasion therefore becomes not just an attack by outsiders, but a disturbing reminder that humanity may not be the most advanced species in the universe.

The Martians’ weaponry is one of Wells’ most striking methods. The Heat-Ray destroys with instant force, giving humans no chance to defend themselves. Wells presents its impact as sudden and absolute, making the violence feel shocking and unfair. Crucially, he does not describe a “battle” in glorious terms. Instead, civilians panic, crowds break apart and destruction happens too quickly for resistance. This removes any sense of heroism and makes the invasion more disturbing because it feels brutally realistic: people are not fighting, they are simply trying to survive.

Wells intensifies the horror through imagery of fire and ruin. Familiar homes and towns are turned into burning wreckage, showing how quickly safety disappears. Fire becomes a repeated symbol of domination, suggesting the Martians can erase human life and civilisation with ease. Wells’ descriptive language often emphasises spread and scale, creating the impression that destruction multiplies too quickly to be controlled. The result is an invasion that feels apocalyptic, as if the landscape itself is being rewritten by violence.

The fighting-machines also make the invasion terrifying. Wells portrays these tripods as towering over the land, using their size to reduce humans to insignificant figures. Their movement is described as unnatural and fast, giving them the energy of predators rather than ordinary machines. Wells blurs the boundary between monster and technology, which makes them more frightening because they seem both mechanical and alive. Their dominance over the landscape reinforces the idea that humans are physically and intellectually outmatched.

Form plays a major role in making the invasion vivid. The novel is told through a first-person narrator, and this creates immediacy. Wells does not give the reader a calm, all-knowing overview: instead, we experience the invasion through a witness who is confused, frightened and overwhelmed. This limited viewpoint makes the invasion feel chaotic and unpredictable, because the narrator only understands events as they unfold. His fear becomes the reader’s fear, and the invasion feels more real because it is filtered through personal shock rather than distant reporting.

Wells also uses structure to show invasion as the collapse of authority and order. Human weapons and armies repeatedly fail to stop the Martians, undermining confidence in civilisation’s strength. As the invasion spreads, society breaks down into panic and flight, and the narrator becomes a witness to disorder replacing control. Wells shows that invasion is not only the destruction of buildings, but the destruction of stability itself.

Ultimately, Wells makes the invasion most horrifying through the Martians’ cold indifference. They show no pity and no moral restraint, treating humans as obstacles rather than individuals. This emotional detachment makes the invasion feel even more hopeless, because it suggests humans cannot appeal to reason or compassion.

In conclusion, Wells strikingly depicts the Martian invasion through suspenseful pacing, terrifying imagery and the immediacy of first-person form. By showing rapid destruction, failed resistance and human panic, Wells creates a powerful vision of civilisation collapsing.

> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The argument is effectively shaped around Wells’ language, structure and form, with a strong sense of how the invasion escalates from curiosity to panic. Read this passage, and then answer the question that follows it: | The fighting was beginning. Almost immediately unseen batteries across the river to our right, unseen because of the trees, took up the chorus, firing heavily one after the other. A woman screamed. Everyone stood arrested by the sudden stir of battle, near us and yet invisible to us. Nothing was to be seen save flat meadows, cows feeding unconcernedly for the most part, and silvery pollard willows motionless in the warm sunlight.

‘The sojers’ll stop ’em,’ said a woman beside me, doubtfully. A haziness rose over the tree-tops.

Then suddenly we saw a rush of smoke far away up the river, a puff of smoke that jerked up into the air and hung; and forthwith the ground heaved underfoot and a heavy explosion shook the air, smashing two or three windows in the houses near, and leaving us astonished.

‘Here they are!’ shouted a man in a blue jersey. ‘Yonder! D’yer see them? Yonder!’

Quickly, one after the other, one, two, three, four of the armoured Martians appeared, far away over the little trees, across the flat meadows that stretch towards Chertsey, and striding hurriedly towards the river. Little cowled figures they seemed at first, going with a rolling motion and as fast as flying birds.

Then, advancing obliquely towards us, came a fifth. Their armoured bodies glittered in the sun as they swept swiftly forward upon the guns, growing rapidly larger as they drew nearer. One on the extreme left, the remotest that is, flourished a huge case high in the air, and the ghostly, terrible Heat-Ray I had already seen on Friday night smote towards Chertsey and struck the town.

At sight of these strange, swift, and terrible creatures the crowd near the water’s edge seemed to me to be for a moment horror-struck. There was no screaming or shouting, but a silence. Then a hoarse murmur and a movement of feet – a splashing from the water. A man, too frightened to drop the portmanteau he carried on his shoulder, swung round and sent me staggering with a blow from the corner of his burden. A woman thrust at me with her hand and rushed past me. I turned, with the rush of the people, but I was not too terrified for thought. The terrible Heat-Ray was in my mind. To get under water! That was it!

‘Get under water!’ I shouted, unheeded.

I faced about again, and rushed towards the approaching Martian, rushed right down the gravelly beach and headlong into the water. Others did the same. A boatload of people putting back came leaping out as I rushed past. The stones under my feet were muddy and slippery, and the river was so low that I ran perhaps twenty feet scarcely waist-deep. Then, as the Martian towered overhead scarcely a couple of hundred yards away, I flung myself forward under the surface. The splashes of the people in the boats leaping into the river sounded like thunderclaps in my ears. People were landing hastily on both sides of the river.

(from Book 1, Chapter 12) | |---| How does Wells make this such a powerful moment in the novel? Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In this extract Wells makes the moment powerfully dramatic by showing the Martian invasion erupting into ordinary life with terrifying speed.  The moment is powerful because the reader experiences the invasion as immediate, chaotic and overwhelming.

Wells begins by building tension through uncertainty. The “unseen batteries” across the river are described as “unseen because of the trees”, and the repetition of “unseen” emphasises confusion and vulnerability. The battle is “near us and yet invisible”, which makes it more frightening because neither the narrator nor the crowd can fully grasp what is happening. The short sentence “A woman screamed” breaks the descriptive flow, creating a sudden emotional jolt and signalling the first crack in public calm.

He then strengthens the moment through a striking contrast between peaceful countryside and violent warfare. The narrator describes “flat meadows”, “cows feeding unconcernedly” and “silvery pollard willows motionless in the warm sunlight”. This gentle, pastoral imagery creates a sense of safety and normality, which makes the invasion feel more shocking when it interrupts it. The cows being “unconcernedly” calm is significant because nature continues as if nothing is wrong, while humans are overwhelmed. Wells uses this contrast to show how fragile human security is.

When the Martians appear, Wells uses structure and pacing to intensify fear. The sequence “one, two, three, four” creates the effect of rapid multiplication, making the enemy seem overwhelming in number and speed. At first they appear as “little cowled figures”, which briefly makes them seem distant or even deceptively small. However, Wells quickly expands the threat by describing their “armoured bodies” and how they move “as fast as flying birds”. The simile suggests unnatural speed, making them feel less like living creatures and more like advanced machines. The invasion becomes powerful here because the reader sees the enemy grow from distant shapes into unstoppable attackers.

Wells adds further horror through the Heat-Ray. It is described as “ghostly” and “terrible”, language that suggests something supernatural and unstoppable rather than human technology. The verb “smote” gives the attack a violent, punishing force, as though the town is being struck down. The narrator’s memory that he has “already seen” the Heat-Ray intensifies tension because he understands what is coming before the crowd does. Wells creates power through anticipation: the reader shares the narrator’s dread.

The crowd’s reaction also makes the moment powerful because Wells captures shock turning into panic with realism. The people become “horror-struck”, followed by a moment of silence where there is “no screaming or shouting”. This pause is chilling because it shows fear becoming so intense it freezes movement. Then chaos begins with “a hoarse murmur and a movement of feet”, suggesting panic spreading like a wave. Wells includes disturbing detail, such as the man “too frightened to drop the portmanteau”, showing terror makes people irrational. The narrator is physically struck and “staggering”, which highlights how quickly humans become helpless bodies in a stampede.

The first-person narration increases the emotional intensity. The narrator’s thoughts become urgent and fragmented: “To get under water! That was it!” The exclamation marks convey panic, but also the desperate clarity of survival instinct. His warning “Get under water!” is “unheeded”, showing communication breaks down as fear takes over. Wells presents society collapsing into individual instinct, which makes the moment feel brutal and realistic.

Finally, Wells ends the extract with frantic movement that reinforces the powerlessness of humanity. The narrator “rushed” into the water, and the repetition of action verbs creates speed and desperation. The beach is “muddy and slippery”, suggesting even escape is dangerous. The Martian “towered overhead”, emphasising the terrifying difference in scale between invader and human.

In conclusion, Wells makes this such a powerful moment through contrast, sensory detail and the intensity of first-person fear. The countryside becomes a battlefield, panic spreads through the crowd and the Martians appear as unstoppable forces.

Read this passage, and then answer the question that follows it: | The crowd swayed a little, and I elbowed my way through. Everyone seemed greatly excited. I heard a peculiar humming sound from the pit. ‘I say!’ said Ogilvy; ‘help keep these idiots back. We don’t know what’s in the confounded thing, you know!’

I saw a young man, a shop assistant in Woking I believe he was, standing on the cylinder and trying to scramble out of the hole again. The crowd had pushed him in.

The end of the cylinder was being screwed out from within. Nearly two feet of shining screw projected. Somebody blundered against me, and I narrowly missed being pitched on to the top of the screw. I turned, and as I did so the screw must have come out, for the lid of the cylinder fell upon the gravel with a ringing concussion. I stuck my elbow into the person behind me, and turned my head towards the Thing again. For a moment that circular cavity seemed perfectly black. I had the sunset in my eyes. I think everyone expected to see a man emerge – possibly something a little unlike us terrestrial men, but in all essentials a man. I know I did. But, looking, I presently saw something stirring within the shadow: greyish billowy movements, one above another, and then two luminous discs – like eyes. Then something resembling a little grey snake, about the thickness of a walking-stick, coiled up out of the writhing middle, and wriggled in the air towards me – and then another.

A sudden chill came over me. There was a loud shriek from a woman behind. I half turned, keeping my eyes fixed upon the cylinder still, from which other tentacles were now projecting, and began pushing my way back from the edge of the pit. I saw astonishment giving place to horror on the faces of the people about me. I heard inarticulate exclamations on all sides. There was a general movement backwards. I saw the shopman struggling still on the edge of the pit. I found myself alone, and saw the people on the other side of the pit running off, Stent among them. I looked again at the cylinder, and ungovernable terror gripped me. I stood petrified and staring.

A big greyish rounded bulk, the size, perhaps, of a bear, was rising slowly and painfully out of the cylinder. As it bulged up and caught the light, it glistened like wet leather.

Two large dark-coloured eyes were regarding me steadfastly. The mass that framed them, the head of the thing, was rounded, and had, one might say, a face. There was a mouth under the eyes, the lipless brim of which quivered and panted, and dropped saliva. The whole creature heaved and pulsated convulsively. A lank tentacular appendage gripped the edge of the cylinder, another swayed in the air.

Those who have never seen a living Martian can scarcely imagine the strange horror of its appearance.

(from Book 1, Chapter 4) | |---| How does Wells powerfully create tension at this moment in the novel? Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In this extract from The War of the Worlds, Wells powerfully creates tension by turning public excitement into sudden fear as the Martian begins to emerge from the cylinder. Using first-person narration, disturbing sensory detail and a slow, suspenseful reveal, Wells makes the moment feel claustrophobic and dangerous.

Wells begins by presenting the crowd as unstable and uncontrollable. The opening line, “The crowd swayed a little”, suggests a mass of bodies moving unpredictably, as if panic could break out at any second. The narrator “elbowed” his way through, which makes the scene feel cramped and pressurised. Although the crowd is “greatly excited”, Wells quickly undercuts this with the “peculiar humming sound from the pit”. The adjective “peculiar” suggests something unnatural, and because the sound comes from below it creates dread, as if danger is rising towards them.

Tension increases through Ogilvy’s warning: “help keep these idiots back”. The word “idiots” shows how foolish and careless the crowd is, while “We don’t know what’s in the confounded thing” highlights uncertainty. Wells suggests the crowd treats the cylinder like entertainment, even though it is clearly threatening. This ignorance creates suspense because the reader senses that curiosity will be punished.

Wells then shows how quickly control collapses. A young shop assistant is “standing on the cylinder” because the crowd had “pushed him in”. This detail is disturbing because it reveals the crowd itself as dangerous, sacrificing someone through reckless excitement. Structurally, it also foreshadows the human cost of the invasion: the first victims are not soldiers, but ordinary people trapped by circumstances and stupidity.

The suspense intensifies as Wells describes the cylinder opening slowly from “within”. The end “was being screwed out”, and the “shining screw” projecting suggests mechanical force and inevitability. The narrator “narrowly missed” falling onto it, which adds immediate physical danger. When the lid falls with a “ringing concussion”, Wells uses sharp sound imagery to make the moment feel sudden and irreversible, as if a seal has been broken.

Wells delays the reveal to build further tension. The narrator sees a “perfectly black” cavity, and the darkness makes the threat more frightening because it hides what is coming. He admits he had “the sunset in my eyes”, suggesting blurred vision and vulnerability. This makes the reader share his fear, since he cannot clearly see the danger until it is almost too late.

When the Martian finally begins to appear, Wells’ language becomes increasingly unsettling. The narrator sees “greyish billowy movements”, vague and shapeless, making the creature feel unnatural. Then he describes “two luminous discs – like eyes”, a simile that creates terror because the darkness is suddenly alive and watching. The tentacles are compared to “a little grey snake”, and the verb “wriggled” suggests disgusting, uncontrolled movement. The fact the tentacle reaches “towards me” makes the threat personal, showing the narrator is no longer a spectator.

Wells also builds tension through the crowd’s reaction. A “shriek” from behind signals fear spreading instantly. The narrator sees “astonishment giving place to horror”, and the crowd moves backwards in panic. Crucially, the narrator becomes isolated: “I found myself alone”. This is terrifying because it leaves him exposed at the moment danger becomes real. Wells intensifies the drama as the narrator admits “ungovernable terror gripped me” and he stands “petrified”. These words suggest fear is so extreme it paralyses him, prolonging suspense because he cannot escape.

Finally, the Martian is described in horrifying physical detail. It rises “slowly and painfully”, making it seem real and unstoppable. Its body “glistened like wet leather”, a simile that creates revulsion through texture. Wells focuses on its face: “Two large dark-coloured eyes… regarding me steadfastly.” The adverb implies intelligence and intention, making it more frightening than a mindless animal. The mouth “panted” and “dropped saliva”, adding grotesque detail that turns fear into disgust. The final line claims its appearance creates “strange horror”, reinforcing that the threat is beyond normal experience.

In conclusion, Wells powerfully creates tension through first-person immediacy, suspenseful delay and increasingly disturbing imagery. The reckless crowd, the gradual emergence of the Martian and the narrator’s paralysing fear combine to make the moment intensely frightening and unforgettable.

How does Wells strikingly convey the narrator’s feelings about the Martians?

Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In The War of the Worlds, Wells strikingly conveys the narrator’s feelings about the Martians by charting a powerful emotional journey from curiosity and disbelief to horror and panic. Wells presents the Martians not simply as enemies, but as creatures so alien and powerful that they destroy the narrator’s sense of safety, certainty and human superiority.

At the start of the invasion, the narrator’s feelings are shaped by fascination rather than terror. He approaches the first cylinder with the mindset of a rational observer, sharing the public excitement as people gather to witness something extraordinary. Wells conveys this early attitude through the narrator’s detailed attention to what he can see and hear, as if careful observation will bring understanding and control. This creates dramatic tension because the narrator initially believes the situation can be explained logically.

However, Wells quickly replaces curiosity with unease by emphasising how mysterious and unnatural the Martians’ arrival is. The narrator becomes unsettled by strange mechanical sounds and movements coming from within the cylinder. Wells uses this gradual build-up to show the narrator’s growing suspicion as he realises the object is not simply a scientific wonder but a threat. Darkness and concealment become frightening to him, because he cannot see what is coming. This creates a powerful emotional shift: the narrator begins to sense that he is facing something beyond ordinary experience, and his feelings change from interest to dread.

When the Martians finally appear, Wells conveys the narrator’s horror through vivid and repulsive imagery. The Martians are not presented as heroic or human-like, but as grotesque and disturbing, with their bodies and movements designed to provoke revulsion. The narrator’s feelings are not just fear of violence, but fear of the unknown: he cannot relate to them as fellow beings. Wells emphasises this through language that focuses on unnatural texture, motion and behaviour, making the Martians seem both animalistic and alien. By making the narrator describe them in such detail, Wells shows him trying to process the unthinkable, even as his body responds instinctively with shock and disgust.

Wells also conveys fear through the narrator’s physical reactions, which make the terror more intense. Moments of shock are often presented as immediate sensations, such as chills, paralysis or breathless panic. This makes the narrator’s feelings believable because they are rooted in the body, not just the mind. Wells frequently shows the narrator frozen or overwhelmed before he forces himself to move, capturing the way real fear can disable someone. These moments create striking tension because the narrator knows he must escape, but his fear delays him, making danger feel even closer.

As the invasion continues, Wells conveys the narrator’s growing helplessness and despair. The narrator repeatedly witnesses the failure of human authority and defence, and this shapes his feelings about the Martians as unstoppable forces rather than opponents. Wells shows that human weapons and strategies barely matter against Martian technology, which makes the narrator’s fear deepen into hopelessness. His emotional state becomes dominated by survival instinct, as he begins to act not with confidence but with desperation. The Martians therefore represent not only physical danger but the collapse of human power, which is psychologically devastating for the narrator.

Wells also conveys the narrator’s feelings about the Martians through the way he describes crowds and society collapsing. He witnesses panic spreading as people lose their sense of order, and this amplifies his fear. The narrator is not only frightened of the Martians, but of what human beings become when fear takes over: selfish, irrational and desperate. Moments of stampede and chaos show that the invasion destroys civilisation from the inside as well as the outside. This makes the narrator’s emotional experience even more overwhelming, because he feels surrounded by danger in every direction: from the Martians and from the breakdown of human behaviour.

In conclusion, Wells strikingly conveys the narrator’s feelings  of curiosity, horror, panic and helplessness. By using first-person narration, grotesque imagery, intense sensory detail and scenes of collapsing order, Wells makes the narrator’s fear vivid and convincing.

parts.problemMd:
How far does Achebe encourage you to admire Ekwefi in the novel?

Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In Things Fall Apart, Chinua Achebe encourages a deep admiration for Ekwefi by presenting her as a woman of profound spirit and maternal devotion who refuses to be entirely broken by her environment. While she is subject to the same "heavy hand" that governs Okonkwo’s entire household, Ekwefi is distinguished by her agency and her capacity for enduring love. Through her history of trauma and her defiant protection of her daughter, Ezinma, Achebe presents her as a character whose internal strength often eclipses the performative masculinity of her husband.

Initially, Achebe encourages admiration through Ekwefi’s independent spirit and her history of following her heart. Unlike other wives who may have been assigned to their husbands, Ekwefi "ran away" from her first husband because she was captivated by Okonkwo when he "threw the Cat" in his youth. This decision illustrates a level of personal autonomy that is rare in her society. Furthermore, she possesses a courageous tongue that few others in Umuofia dare to use against Okonkwo. When he beats her for a perceived slight against a banana tree, she has the "audacity" to murmur a taunt about "guns that never shot," even after he has already used his fists. Achebe uses this incident to show that while Okonkwo can control her body through violence, he cannot suppress her defiant personality.

The most striking reason to admire Ekwefi is her fierce maternal instinct, which Achebe portrays as a form of heroic endurance. Having borne ten children and lost nine of them in infancy, Ekwefi’s life is defined by a "grim resignation" that eventually transforms into an intense, companionable bond with her only surviving child, Ezinma. Achebe describes their relationship as one of "equals," strengthened by "little conspiracies" such as eating eggs in the secrecy of the bedroom. This bond reaches a climax when Chielo, the priestess of Agbala, carries Ezinma away into the night. Despite her "terror" of the dark and the voice of the priestess which was "clear as metal," Ekwefi follows them through the forest, driven by a sudden strength that makes her "like a hen whose only chick has been carried away by a kite". Her vow to "defend her against all the gods in the world" and to "die with her" if necessary provides the most admirable image of courage in the novel.

However, Achebe does not sugar coat her character, noting that her suffering has made her "a very bitter woman". Her inability to rejoice with Nwoye’s mother over the birth of sons reveals the deep psychological toll of her "evil chi". This complexity makes her more human and, arguably, more admirable, as her love for Ezinma persists despite this internal "cloud on her brow".

In conclusion, Achebe encourages the reader to admire Ekwefi not because she is a saintly figure, but because she is a resilient survivor. By contrasting her genuine, selfless courage during the night of the priestess with Okonkwo’s later "manly" and "reasonable" arrival at the cave, Achebe suggests that true strength is found in those who protect what they love, regardless of the personal cost.

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **Commentary**

> The essay demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Ekwefi's internal world, particularly the trauma of losing nine children and how this shapes her relationship with Ezinma. The response explores the imagery of the "hen" and the "kite" and the contrast between Ekwefi's "audacity" and Okonkwo's "heavy hand" in detail, showing deep engagement with how the writer achieves their effects.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Analyse how the **“egg conspiracy”** serves as a **microcosm** of the **private world** Ekwefi creates to **elude** the **patriarchal restrictions** of the **compound**
> - Use the **Chielo sequence** to discuss the difference between **physical courage** and **emotional** or **spiritual courage**
> - Explore how the term **“ogbanje”** functions as a **structural device** to explain Ekwefi’s **bitterness** and **“grim resignation”**
> - Highlight the significance of Ekwefi’s decision to **run away** to **Okonkwo** as an act of **agency** that sets her apart from **other wives**

An iron gong sounded, setting up a wave of expectation in the crowd. Everyone looked in the direction of the *egwugwu* house. *Gome, gome, gome, gome* went the gong, and a powerful flute blew a high-pitched blast. Then came the voices of the *egwugwu*, guttural and awesome. The wave struck the women and children and there was a backward stampede. But it was momentary, They were already far enough where they stood and there was room for running away if any of the *egwugwu* should go towards them.

The drum sounded again and the flute blew. The *egwugwu* house was now a pandemonium of quavering voices: *Aru oyim de de de dei*! filled the air as the spirits of the ancestors , just emerged from the earth, greeted themselves in their esoteric language. The *egwugwu* house into which they emerged faced the forest, away from the crowd, who saw only its back with the many-colored patterns and drawings done by specially chosen women at regular intervals. These women never saw the inside of the hut. No woman ever did. They scrubbed and painted the outside walls under the supervision of men. If they imagined what was inside, they kept their imagination to themselves. No woman ever asked questions about the most powerful and the most secret cult in the clan.

*Aru oyim de de de dei*! flew around the dark, closed hut like tongues of fire. The ancestral spirits of the clan were abroad.

The metal gong beat continuously now and the flute, shrill and powerful, floated on the chaos.

And then the *egwugwu* appeared. The women and children sent up a great shout and took to their heels. It was instinctive. A woman fled as soon as an *egwugwu* came in sight. And when, as on that day, nine of the greatest masked spirits in the clan came out together it was a terrifying spectacle. Even Mgbafo took to her heels and had to be restrained by her brothers.

Each of the nine *egwugwu* represented a village of the clan. Their leader was called Evil Forest. Smoke poured out of his head.

(*from* Chapter 10) | |---| In what ways does Achebe make this a dramatic and emotionally gripping moment? Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In this passage from Chapter 10 of Things Fall Apart, Chinua Achebe makes the ceremony of the egwugwu a dramatic and emotionally gripping moment by masterfully building tension through sensory imagery and the depiction of communal terror. By contrasting the mundane chatter of the village with the sudden, sudden intrusion of the ancestral spirits, Achebe creates a scene where the boundaries between the living and the dead are blurred. Through onomatopoeia, visceral physical reactions, and the striking visual of Evil Forest, the author ensures the reader experiences the same fearful reverence as the Umuofian crowd.

Initially, Achebe builds drama by establishing a sense of anticipation through the soundscape of the village. He describes the crowd’s noise as a "deep rumble carried by the wind," comparing it to the familiar sounds of the "market". This creates an emotionally gripping effect because it sets a baseline of normal human activity before the supernatural elements intrude. The drama intensifies with the sudden sounding of the "iron gong" and the onomatopoeic "Gome, gome, gome, gome," which signals a sharp shift in the atmosphere. Achebe uses the "high-pitched blast" of the flute and the "guttural and awesome" voices of the egwugwu to signal that the spirits have emerged, moving the scene from the secular to the sacred in a way that feels sudden and overwhelming.

Achebe makes the moment emotionally gripping by focusing on the physical terror of the spectators, particularly the women and children. The personified wave that "struck the women and children", with the "backward stampede" and the fact that they "took to their heels" when the egwugwu appeared highlights the perceived danger and spiritual gravity of the event. This reaction is described as "instinctive," suggesting that the fear is deeply rooted in the culture’s psyche. The drama is further heightened by the description of the egwugwu house as a "pandemonium of quavering voices" where the esoteric greeting "Aru oyim de de de dei!" fills the air. The spirits are described as flying around the hut like "tongues of fire," a metaphor that conveys a sense of volatile, unearthly power.

The climax of the passage provides a striking visual conclusion that is both dramatic and memorable. The emergence of the nine masked spirits, each representing a village, culminates in the introduction of their leader, "Evil Forest". Achebe uses a singular, haunting image to cement the gripping nature of the scene: "Smoke poured out of his head". This detail serves as a physical manifestation of the spirit’s power and authority, separating him from the "bodies" of the humans present. By ending the passage on this supernatural image, Achebe confirms that the trial is not merely a legal proceeding but a spiritual reckoning, leaving the audience in a state of breathless suspense.

In conclusion, Achebe makes this moment dramatic and emotionally gripping by utilising a crescendo of aural and visual effects. Through the use of rhythmic percussion, the depiction of communal panic, and the horrific imagery of the smoking ancestral leader, he captures the absolute authority of the egwugwu. The passage reveals that in Umuofia, justice is a public, spiritual, and deeply frightening performance that binds the clan together through shared awe.

parts.problemMd:
Explore the ways Achebe reveals the pressures and expectations placed on boys and young men in Things Fall Apart.

Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In Things Fall Apart, Chinua Achebe reveals that the pressures and expectations placed on boys and young men are defined by an uncompromising ideal of masculinity that demands the total suppression of emotion and the pursuit of material success. Through the domestic tyranny of Okonkwo and the internal struggle of his son, Nwoye, Achebe portrays Umuofia as a society where "manliness" is a performative burden. The author suggests that these expectations, rooted in the fear of being seen as "weak" or "lazy," ultimately alienate the next generation and contribute to the fracturing of the clan.

Achebe initially establishes that the primary expectation for a young man is to distance himself from any resemblance to a failure. For Okonkwo, this pressure stems from his father, Unoka, who was "lazy and improvident" and "incapable of thinking about tomorrow". Consequently, Okonkwo "ruled his household with a heavy hand," and his children lived in "perpetual fear of his fiery temper". This pressure is most visible in his treatment of Nwoye. At only twelve years old, Nwoye causes his father "great anxiety for his incipient laziness," leading Okonkwo to "correct him by constant nagging and beating". Through this, Achebe reveals that childhood for an Umuofian boy is not a period of innocence, but a rigorous apprenticeship in "manliness," where any perceived softness is met with violence.

The author further explores these expectations through the symbolic division of labour and the celebration of physical prowess. Success for a young man is measured by his ability to provide, specifically through the cultivation of "yam, the king of crops". Boys are expected to master "difficult and masculine tasks," such as "splitting wood" or "pounding food". Achebe shows that Nwoye learns to "feign annoyance" when asked to help with "women's troubles," because he knows it pleases his father to see him "grumbling about women". This performance of misogyny is presented as a necessary survival mechanism. By showing Nwoye pretending that he "no longer cared for women's stories" in favour of Okonkwo’s "masculine stories of violence and bloodshed," Achebe highlights the psychological cost of these societal expectations.

Finally, Achebe reveals the tragic consequences when these pressures become unsustainable. The expectation that "to show affection was a sign of weakness" leads Okonkwo to participate in the killing of Ikemefuna, the boy who "called him father". This act of performative strength is the breaking point for Nwoye, who feels "something seemed to give way inside him, like the snapping of a tightened bow". Achebe’s use of the "Roaring Flame" metaphor to describe Okonkwo’s masculinity provides a definitive critique of these pressures: "Living fire begets cold, impotent ash". The expectation for Nwoye to be a "flaming fire" like his father results instead in his total conversion to a new faith, suggesting that the rigid expectations of Umuofian manhood are what truly cause the "center" to fail.

In conclusion, Achebe reveals that the expectations placed on young men in Umuofia are rooted in a destructive cycle of fear and performance. By presenting masculinity as a "heavy hand" that crushes individual sensitivity, he shows how the clan’s insistence on toughness and achievement creates a spiritual vacuum. Ultimately, the novel suggests that a society which demands the murder of affection in its sons is one that has already begun to fall apart from within.

The response explores the imagery of the "snapping bow" and the "Roaring Flame" in detail, showing deep engagement with how language reveals the psychological damage inflicted on young men. The analysis of the "women’s stories" versus "masculine stories" is interpreted effectively as a conflict of identity. Quotations are precise, well-chosen, and integrated with flair.

parts.problemMd:
How does Achebe vividly convey the tensions between individual desires and community values in Things Fall Apart?

Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In Things Fall Apart, Chinua Achebe vividly conveys the tension between individual desires and community values by presenting Umuofia as a society where personal ambition must constantly be reconciled with rigid ancestral laws. Through the protagonist Okonkwo, Achebe explores how an individual's "passionate" desire for status can lead to the subversion of communal harmony. By contrasting Okonkwo’s performative masculinity with the more nuanced spiritual demands of the clan, Achebe reveals that the centre of the community is often destabilised as much by internal individual failings as by external colonial forces.

Initially, Achebe establishes this tension through Okonkwo’s violation of the "Week of Peace". While the community values this sacred period as a time when "a man does not say a harsh word to his neighbor" to honour the "great goddess of the earth," Okonkwo’s individual fiery temper takes precedence. His desire to exert domestic control leads him to beat his youngest wife, an act that the priest Ezeani identifies as a "great evil" that could "ruin the whole clan". Achebe uses this incident to show that Okonkwo’s individual desire for dominance is fundamentally at odds with the communal need for spiritual equilibrium. The tension is vividly conveyed through the dialogue of the elders, who note that even in cases of extreme individual provocation, the community value of "peace" must remain inviolable.

The author further explores these tensions through the tragic sacrifice of Ikemefuna. The "Oracle of the Hills and the Caves" decrees the boy's death, representing a communal and spiritual mandate that Okonkwo individualistically chooses to carry out personally, despite the warning from Ezeudu: "That boy calls you father. Do not bear a hand in his death". Here, the tension lies between Okonkwo’s individual "fear of failure and of weakness" and the community’s expectation of balanced justice. By showing Okonkwo "dazed with fear" as he "cut him down," Achebe reveals that Okonkwo is not motivated by communal duty, but by a private, desperate need to prove his own "manliness". This act alienates him from his son Nwoye and creates a "snapping" of the familial bond that mirrors the eventual fracturing of the clan itself.

Finally, Achebe reveals the tension through the character of Nwoye, whose individual "desire" for a more compassionate spiritual path leads to a total rejection of Umuofian values. Nwoye is haunted by the communal practice of leaving twins to die in the "Evil Forest," a custom that fills his soul with a "vague and persistent question". When the missionaries arrive, it is the "poetry of the new religion" that captures Nwoye, offering him an individual "relief" from the "heavy hand" of his father’s and the community’s expectations. Achebe’s concluding metaphor for this tension is strikingly bleak: "Living fire begets cold, impotent ash". The community’s insistence on a hyper-masculine ideal—Okonkwo’s "fire"—ultimately produces an individual reaction that destroys the very continuity the community sought to preserve.

In conclusion, Achebe conveys these tensions by presenting individuals who are unable to find a middle ground between their internal drives and the external laws of their people. Whether it is Okonkwo’s "inflexible will" or Nwoye’s quiet "conspiracy" of dissent, Achebe suggests that a community which cannot accommodate the complex desires of its members is one that is destined to fall apart.

The response explores the imagery of the "snapping bow" and "living fire" in detail, showing deep engagement with how language reveals the psychological cost of societal pressures.

> - Discuss the significance of the **“Oracle”** to show how **communal values** are often presented as **absolute** and beyond **individual negotiation**
> - Explore the **“yam” imagery** as a **symbol** of the **individual’s struggle** for **status** within the community’s **economic framework**
> - Highlight how Achebe uses the character of **Obierika** as a **“voice of reason”** to provide a **balanced perspective** on the tension between **law** and **conscience**

parts.problemMd:
Read this passage carefully, and then answer the question that follows it. Ikemefuna, a boy who has lived in Okonkwo’s household for three years and calls him father, is being led along a forest path by the men of Umuofia. He does not know that they mean to kill him.

He sang it in his mind, and walked to its beat. If the song ended on his right foot, his mother was alive. If it ended on his left, she was dead. No, not dead, but ill. It ended on the right. She was alive and well. He sang the song again, and it ended on the left. But the second time did not count. The first voice gets to Chukwu, or God’s house. That was a favorite saying of children. Ikemefuna felt like a child once more. It must be the thought of going home to his mother.

** **

One of the men behind him cleared his throat. Ikemefuna looked back, and the man growled at him to go on and not stand looking back. The way he said it sent cold fear down Ikemefuna’s back. His hands trembled vaguely on the black pot he carried. Why had Okonkwo withdrawn to the rear? Ikemefuna felt his legs melting under him. And he was afraid to look back.

** **

As the man who had cleared his throat drew up and raised his machete, Okonkwo looked away. He heard the blow. The pot fell and broke in the sand. He heard Ikemefuna cry, “My father, they have killed me!” as he ran towards him. Dazed with fear, Okonkwo drew his machete and cut him down. He was afraid of being thought weak.

How does Achebe make this such a shocking and powerful moment in the novel?

Remember to support your ideas with details from the writing.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

Achebe makes this a shocking and powerful moment by letting us share Ikemefuna’s innocent hopes right up until the blow falls, and then showing Okonkwo kill him out of fear of looking weak.

The moment is powerful because Achebe puts us inside Ikemefuna’s mind and makes us like him. As he walks, he plays a childhood game, singing a song to himself: “If the song ended on his right foot, his mother was alive.” This small, innocent detail shows how young and trusting he still is and makes him seem vulnerable, and it is painful for the reader because we know something he does not, that he is being led to his death. The line “Ikemefuna felt like a child once more” is heartbreaking, because his happiest, most trusting moment comes just before he is killed. This gap between what he believes and what is really happening creates a strong sense of dramatic irony that makes the scene almost unbearable.

Achebe then builds fear through the change in the men around him. One of the men “cleared his throat” and “growled at him to go on”, and “the way he said it sent cold fear down Ikemefuna’s back.” The physical description of his fear, his “hands trembled” and his “legs melting under him”, shows us how terrified he is and makes us feel the danger with him. The most frightening detail is the question “Why had Okonkwo withdrawn to the rear?”, because we understand the terrible reason even though Ikemefuna is only beginning to sense it. Achebe makes us dread what is coming without stating it directly, so the innocent boy becomes a helpless victim in front of us.

The killing itself is shocking because of how quickly and plainly it is described. When the first man raises “his machete”, Achebe writes simply that “Okonkwo looked away. He heard the blow.” Not seeing it makes it worse, and the sound of “The pot fell and broke in the sand” suggests the violence in a horrible way. Then comes Ikemefuna’s cry, “My father, they have killed me!”, as he runs to Okonkwo for protection. The word “father” is devastating, because he is running to the very man who is about to kill him.

The most powerful part is the final sentence and the reason behind it. Achebe writes, “Dazed with fear, Okonkwo drew his machete and cut him down. He was afraid of being thought weak.” The short, flat sentences make the act feel sudden and cold. What is most disturbing is that Okonkwo does not kill out of anger or belief, but out of fear, fear of seeming weak in front of the other men. This one line in the narrative reveals the flaw that drives Okonkwo throughout the novel: his terror of weakness is stronger than his love for the boy who called him father.

Overall, Achebe makes this moment shocking and powerful by building our sympathy for Ikemefuna, using dramatic irony to fill us with dread, and then describing the killing in short, plain sentences. The final line, “He was afraid of being thought weak”, turns a personal tragedy into the key to Okonkwo’s whole character.

> **Commentary**

Each point names a method — the dramatic irony, the short sentences, the withheld violence — and explains its effect on the reader. parts.problemMd: How does Lee portray Mayella Ewell as an important character in the novel?
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

Mayella Ewell is a central character in To Kill a Mockingbird despite her limited appearance, as her actions catalyse the major conflict in the novel: Tom Robinson’s trial. Through her character, Harper Lee explores themes of prejudice, isolation, class, and injustice.

Mayella is important because she falsely accuses Tom Robinson of raping her, which sets the novel’s main courtroom drama into motion. This accusation drives the tension in the second half of the novel and provides Lee with a powerful lens through which to examine the racism embedded within the legal system and wider society. Without Mayella’s claim, there would be no trial to challenge Atticus Finch’s moral courage or to reveal the extent of Maycomb’s racial prejudices. The trial forces the children, especially Scout and Jem, to confront uncomfortable truths about their community, shifting their understanding of morality and justice.

Lee also uses Mayella to complicate the theme of prejudice by showing that she is not only a perpetrator but also a victim. As the eldest daughter of the violent and abusive Bob Ewell, Mayella is responsible for caring for her many younger siblings after the death of their mother. Her life is defined by poverty, isolation, and fear. Scout, despite her dislike of Mayella, recognises this, saying, “Mayella Ewell must have been the loneliest person in the world.” This insight shows how Lee encourages readers to view Mayella with a degree of sympathy, even though her actions are morally indefensible. She is a young woman trapped by circumstance, gender expectations, and social class, which adds complexity to her character and emphasises how prejudice operates across different levels.

Mayella’s role in the trial highlights the rigid racial and social hierarchies in 1930s Southern America. Although the Ewells are seen as "absolute trash" and are among the lowest in Maycomb’s social order, Mayella’s whiteness still places her above Tom Robinson, a black man. This power imbalance enables her accusation to be taken seriously despite clear evidence of Tom’s innocence. Lee uses Mayella to show how deeply racial prejudice is embedded in society — so much so that a white girl’s word automatically outweighs the truth told by a black man. Tom’s only "crime" is feeling sorry for Mayella, which the jury sees as a breach of social boundaries: a black man daring to pity a white woman is unacceptable within Maycomb’s racist values.

However, Lee is also careful to suggest that Mayella’s accusation stems from fear and desperation rather than outright cruelty. When Tom testifies that Mayella kissed him and was caught by her father, it becomes clear that her actions are an attempt to cover up her own breach of racial taboos. In the harsh world she lives in, the punishment for a white woman showing affection to a black man would be severe, particularly from her father, who is implied to be abusive. Tom claims Bob Ewell shouted, “you goddamn whore, I’ll kill ya”, which suggests Mayella may have accused Tom to protect herself from violence. This portrayal creates a sense of tragedy: Mayella sacrifices Tom to survive, further underlining how systemic racism and patriarchy trap individuals in cycles of harm.

Lee adds another layer of complexity to Mayella’s character through her love of beauty and order, seen in the red geraniums she grows outside her run-down home. These flowers suggest a desire for something better than her current life allows. They symbolise a longing for dignity and gentleness in a world that offers her neither. This small detail invites readers to consider the contrast between who Mayella is and who she might have been in a different environment, deepening the sense of wasted potential and reinforcing the novel’s wider critique of injustice.

In conclusion, Mayella Ewell is important not only because she triggers the events that shape the narrative, but because she represents the tangled web of prejudice, poverty and patriarchy. Through her, Lee illustrates how individuals can be both victims and perpetrators of injustice, and how systems of inequality produce tragic outcomes. Mayella’s story reminds us that justice is not always blind, and that truth alone is often not enough to overcome the weight of social prejudice.

These are integrated into a sustained argument that keeps a clear focus on Mayella’s significance.

The response engages sensitively with Lee’s methods, particularly through analysis of dialogue, power imbalance and symbolism such as the red geraniums. parts.problemMd: How does Lee vividly explore the theme of prejudice in the novel?
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In To Kill a Mockingbird, Harper Lee explores the theme of prejudice in many forms — racial, social, and gender-based — showing how deeply embedded it is within the community of Maycomb. Through the experiences of Scout, the trial of Tom Robinson, and the treatment of Boo Radley, Lee critiques the injustice and irrationality of prejudice in 1930s America.

The most obvious and devastating form of prejudice in the novel is racial discrimination. Tom Robinson, a black man, is falsely accused of raping Mayella Ewell, a white woman. Although Atticus presents strong evidence that Tom is innocent, the all-white jury convicts him purely because of the colour of his skin. Tom’s only “mistake” is saying that he felt sorry for Mayella, an expression of empathy that Maycomb’s white community views as offensive and presumptuous. This reaction exposes the rigid racial hierarchy of the town in the Jim Crow era, where black people are expected to remain not only separate (due to segregation) but also subservient. As Scout later reflects, “Atticus had used every tool available to free men to save Tom Robinson, but in the secret courts of men’s hearts, Atticus had no case.” Lee’s use of irony here underlines the tragic consequences of racial bias.

Lee further explores the consequences of racial prejudice through characters like Dolphus Raymond. He pretends to be an alcoholic to explain his choice to live with a black woman and mixed-race children. In reality, he drinks Coca-Cola from a paper bag and only pretends to be drunk to give people an excuse they can understand. Raymond tells Scout, “they could never, never understand that I live like I do because that’s the way I want to live.” His actions highlight the pressure to conform to societal norms and the lengths people go to in order to protect themselves from judgement.

Social prejudice is also portrayed through the class divisions in Maycomb. Aunt Alexandra is deeply class-conscious and believes that people should only associate with those of the same social standing. She disapproves of Scout’s friendship with Walter Cunningham, declaring he is “not our kind of folks.” Through Aunt Alexandra, Lee criticises the rigid social hierarchy of the Deep South, where even white families are judged by their wealth and family history. Her hypocritical nature is further exposed during her missionary circle meeting. The ladies express sympathy for the Mruna tribe in Africa while simultaneously making derogatory remarks about the black community in their own town. This moment starkly reveals the disconnect between their public charity and private prejudice.

Another victim of prejudice is Boo Radley, who becomes the subject of fear and gossip simply because he lives a reclusive life. Children in the town, including Scout and Jem, initially see Boo as a “malevolent phantom” and he is blamed for any strange event in Maycomb. However, by the end of the novel, Boo is revealed to be gentle and kind, quietly protecting the children by leaving them gifts and eventually saving them from Bob Ewell. Scout’s growing empathy is captured when she finally meets Boo and says that “he was real nice” and Atticus responds, “Most people are, Scout, when you finally see them.” This moment encapsulates Lee’s central message that prejudice often stems from ignorance and fear of the unknown.

Gender prejudice is another key theme, particularly through Scout’s experiences. As a tomboy, she resists traditional expectations of femininity. She is often told to behave more “ladylike”, especially by Aunt Alexandra, and is excluded from playing with Jem and Dill simply for being a girl. Even as a child, Scout recognises the limitations placed on her because of her gender. Lee uses Scout’s narrative voice to expose the absurdity of such social expectations and to suggest that gender roles are another form of harmful prejudice in Maycomb society.

In conclusion, Lee presents prejudice as a destructive and pervasive force within Maycomb. By exploring racial, social, and gender discrimination, she challenges readers to confront their own biases and consider the harm caused by ignorance and injustice. Through the eyes of Scout, the reader learns that prejudice is not only wrong, but deeply ingrained — and that change begins with understanding and empathy.

> This response would be placed in the highest band. It shows a confident and detailed exploration of how Harper Lee vividly presents the theme of prejudice throughout the novel.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The candidate demonstrates strong knowledge of the text, using a wide range of well-selected quotations and references to explore racial, social and gender prejudice. Key characters and episodes, including Tom Robinson, Dolphus Raymond, Boo Radley and Aunt Alexandra, are used effectively to show how prejudice operates across different areas of Maycomb society.
> 
> There is clear insight in the way the essay explores both the causes and consequences of prejudice. The response engages sensitively with Lee’s methods, particularly through analysis of irony, contrast and Scout’s narrative voice. Ideas are well developed and consistently linked to the question.
> 
> Overall, this is a perceptive, well-structured and well-supported response that shows strong personal engagement with the text.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep a clear focus on **how** prejudice is presented and **how vividly** it is explored
> - Use **key characters and events** to show different forms of prejudice
> - Analyse how Lee uses **narrative voice, irony and contrast** to shape the reader’s response
> - Support ideas with **short quotations** and precise references to the text
> - Explore both the **causes and effects** of prejudice on individuals and the community

parts.problemMd: Explore how Lee presents the experience of growing up in To Kill a Mockingbird.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In To Kill a Mockingbird, Harper Lee explores the experience of growing up through Scout and Jem’s moral and emotional development. The novel, a bildungsroman, traces their journey from innocence to a deeper understanding of their society, its injustices and their place within it. Set in the fictional town of Maycomb during the 1930s, the novel uses events such as the trial of Tom Robinson, interactions with Boo Radley and lessons from Atticus to show how children grow up by facing uncomfortable truths and by learning empathy.

At the beginning of the novel, Scout is presented as an innocent and imaginative child. Her world is filled with childish superstitions and confusion. She believes Boo Radley is a “malevolent phantom” and is terrified of him without ever having seen him. Her misunderstanding of words like “Absolute Morphodite” and her scorn for Miss Caroline’s teaching methods reflect her immaturity and naivety. These moments show how Scout sees the world in simple, black-and-white terms, unaware of the complexity of human behaviour or society’s expectations. Harper Lee uses Scout’s humorous misunderstandings and childlike perspective to highlight how children start life innocently, absorbing the values and prejudices of those around them.

As Scout grows, she begins to confront Maycomb’s flawed social values, especially during Tom Robinson’s trial. The racist treatment of Tom by Mr Gilmer shocks both Dill and Scout. When Dill begins to cry at the injustice, Mr Raymond tells Scout he is still a child — that he will eventually learn not to react and will simply conform to society’s expectations as he grows up. This moment is a turning point in the children’s development as it shows how growing up in Maycomb means being pressured to accept prejudice as normal. However, Scout resists this, and by the end of the novel, she still retains her empathy, showing Lee’s hope for the next generation.

Atticus plays a central role in teaching Scout and Jem how to grow up morally. His advice to “climb into” another man’s “skin and walk around in it” teaches Scout to develop empathy, which signals her growing maturity. This lesson comes full circle when Scout finally meets Boo Radley. Instead of fearing him, she recognises his kindness and protects his identity, standing on the Radley porch and seeing the world from his point of view. This moment symbolises Scout’s emotional growth: she has moved from superstition to understanding, from childish innocence to compassion.

Jem’s growing up is also a key part of the novel. He begins to distance himself from Scout, insisting she act more mature and sometimes criticising her with comments like “you’re gettin’ more like a girl every day!” His annoyance at childish behaviour signals his transition into adolescence. Further, the trial deeply affects him, shattering his belief in the goodness of Maycomb’s people. The Jim Crow laws legalised segregation and events like the Scottsboro trials inspired the trial of Tom Robinson. When the jury finds Tom Robinson guilty, Jem is devastated and begins to understand the depth of injustice in their community. Jem’s new awareness of the world’s unfairness shows his moral growth, but also his loss of innocence. Lee uses their growth to criticise these injustices while offering hope that the next generation might challenge them.

Gender expectations also shape Scout’s development. Aunt Alexandra disapproves of Scout’s tomboy nature and wants her to act like a “lady”. She criticises Scout for wearing dungarees and discourages her from playing with the boys. These pressures reflect the 1930s Southern setting, where strict gender roles defined women’s behaviour. However, Lee presents Scout’s resistance as admirable, suggesting that growing up does not mean conforming to unjust expectations. Scout begins to realise that she can learn from Alexandra while still maintaining her sense of identity, showing a more mature understanding of compromise.

In conclusion, To Kill a Mockingbird explores growing up as a process of gaining moral awareness, developing empathy and questioning societal norms. Through Scout and Jem, Lee shows how children grow not just physically, but emotionally and ethically, especially when faced with the harsh realities of injustice.

parts.problemMd: How does Lee make Aunt Alexandra a vivid and memorable character in the novel?
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

Aunt Alexandra is a complex, memorable and important character in To Kill a Mockingbird as she represents the traditional Southern values of class, gender and racial hierarchy. Through her character, Harper Lee explores ideas of family, prejudice and social conformity. Alexandra both challenges and reinforces the values of Maycomb and her evolving relationship with Scout adds depth to the novel’s treatment of gender and moral awareness.

When Aunt Alexandra first arrives in Maycomb, she is immediately portrayed as imposing and controlling. Her first words are commands: “Put my bag in the front bedroom, Calpurnia… Jean Louise, stop scratching your head”. This shows her need for order and her desire to establish authority within the Finch household. Scout feels imprisoned by her aunt’s expectations, describing her arrival as the moment she “felt the starched walls of a pink cotton penitentiary closing in”. The use of prison imagery illustrates Scout’s resistance to Alexandra’s attempts to impose traditional femininity. Lee presents Alexandra as a product of her time: conventional, proper and deeply concerned with reputation.

Aunt Alexandra is obsessed with family heritage and social status. She believes that “fine folks” are those who have lived on the same land for generations, asserting that “the longer a family had been squatting on one patch of land the finer it was”. This narrow view reflects the rigid class system of the 1930s Deep South, where family history determined social worth. Scout observes that her aunt would “point out the shortcomings of other tribal groups to the greater glory of our own”, which highlights Alexandra’s snobbery and blind loyalty to her social circle.

Her views on class and race are also closely linked. When Scout wants to invite Walter Cunningham to their house, Aunt Alexandra is horrified, saying “he — is — trash” and warning that associating with such people will cause Scout and Jem to pick up their “habits”. This moment reveals Alexandra’s class prejudice and her belief that children should be protected from inferior influences. Likewise, she is disturbed by the children’s close relationship with Calpurnia. Alexandra insists that Calpurnia is no longer needed and is shocked to learn the children have attended her church.

Despite her prejudice, Aunt Alexandra is also presented as caring. She eventually allows Calpurnia to serve her missionary guests after recognising her grace and competence. This small concession signals a softening of her rigid views. Additionally, although she initially believes Atticus’ defence of Tom Robinson brings shame to the family, she shows genuine concern when Tom is killed. Her asking Atticus if the town’s criticism upsets him reveals her inner conflict and perhaps guilt. This emotional moment highlights how even those steeped in prejudice can experience doubt and change.

Aunt Alexandra’s character development is especially visible in her relationship with Scout. Initially, she tries to make Scout behave like a “young lady” criticising her dungarees and tomboy habits. She urges Scout to embrace embroidery and activities that will improve her reputation, such as organising missionary teas. However, by the end of the novel, when Scout is attacked by Bob Ewell, Alexandra’s protective side emerges. She calls Scout “darling” and even brings her overalls, showing a rare moment of acceptance and tenderness. This change suggests that Alexandra begins to value Scout’s individuality over outward appearances.

Scout describes her aunt as having “river-boat, boarding-school manners” and being “an incurable gossip”, yet she also acknowledges that Alexandra “let any moral come along and she would uphold it”. Lee uses these observations to present Alexandra as both comic and serious, as she is someone who clings to outdated customs but also possesses strength and care. She is described as the last of her kind, symbolising the dying values of the Old South that the novel critiques.

In conclusion, Aunt Alexandra is a character who represents the Southern Belle ideal, shaped by a culture of class consciousness, gender expectations and racial prejudice. Through her, Lee examines how these values can be both upheld and questioned within a single individual. Alexandra’s development over the course of the novel, from rigid enforcer of tradition to caring family member, shows that even deeply ingrained beliefs can be challenged by empathy and love.

Aunt Alexandra’s authority, concern with class and reputation, and attitudes towards race and gender are explored in detail, with ideas consistently linked to her impact on Scout and the Finch household.
