> Overall, the essay is well structured and evaluative, ending with a clear conclusion that reinforces the importance of hope and ambition within the play.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep a clear focus on **hope and ambition**, not just dreams or wishes
> - Use **stage directions and symbolism** to show how ambition is presented theatrically
> - Explore how **racism and hardship challenge** characters’ hopes
> - Analyse **character development**, especially moments of loss and renewal
> - Consider how **structure and the ending** reinforce optimism

parts.problemMd:
Explore how Odimba dramatically conveys the impact of the bus boycott  in Princess & The Hustler.

Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In Princess & The Hustler, Chinonyerem Odimba dramatically conveys the impact of the Bristol Bus Boycott by showing how a political struggle shapes everyday life, family relationships and personal identity. Rather than presenting the boycott only as background history, Odimba weaves it directly into the characters’ lives, revealing its emotional cost as well as its power to inspire unity and change. Through dialogue, structure, stage directions and contrasts between characters, the play presents the boycott as a force that transforms both the community and the individual.

One of the most dramatic ways Odimba conveys the boycott’s impact is by showing how it affects the characters’ sense of dignity and belonging. The bus company’s refusal to employ Black workers exposes the racism that limits opportunities for the Windrush generation. This injustice is not presented abstractly. It becomes personal through characters who are expected to accept discrimination quietly. The pressure to “be mindful” reflects how Black families must constantly consider their safety and reputation in a hostile society. This makes the boycott feel necessary and urgent, because it represents a refusal to continue living under silent restriction.

Odimba also highlights the emotional strain the boycott places on family life, particularly through the conflict between Wendell and Mavis. Wendell returns with the swagger of a hustler, attempting to excuse his failures by blaming the lack of respect he receives in Britain. His defensiveness shows how racism has damaged his confidence and sense of purpose. In contrast, Mavis carries the burden of responsibility, raising the children alone and trying to protect them from further instability. Their tense confrontations reflect the way political injustice can deepen personal wounds, creating anger and frustration within families as well as communities. The boycott therefore becomes more than protest. It is part of the characters’ daily survival.

The impact of the boycott is also conveyed through Junior, who is presented as torn between personal responsibility and public action. His reluctance to leave his sisters shows the pressure young people feel to contribute to change while also protecting their families. This conflict dramatises the boycott’s reach, as it does not only belong to adults or activists but affects the next generation as well. Junior’s eventual involvement suggests that the boycott shapes identity by forcing individuals to decide what kind of future they want and what sacrifices they are willing to make.

Most powerfully, Odimba conveys the boycott’s impact through Princess herself, linking political struggle to personal ambition. Princess’ pageant fantasy is not separate from the boycott. It becomes a symbol of resistance, as she insists on her own beauty and worth in a society that devalues Blackness. When she experiences rejection, such as being excluded while Lorna is invited to a party, her sense of identity collapses. Her destruction of her “cupboard world” shows how racism harms children psychologically, making the boycott’s purpose even more significant. It is not only about jobs, but about dignity and self-belief. When Princess later recovers her confidence and demands to be crowned, the play suggests that hope and activism are connected, as both involve refusing to accept imposed limits.

Odimba’s stagecraft also strengthens the dramatic impact of the boycott. The repeated stage directions describing the room “explod[ing] into a world of pageantry” create a visual transformation on stage, showing how imagination and resistance can break through harsh reality. Structurally, the play builds towards moments of collective empowerment, with the boycott’s success announced at the end. This ending creates a sense of victory and release, not only for the characters but for the audience, because the struggle results in real change. By intertwining the boycott’s outcome with the family’s movement towards unity, Odimba suggests that political action can heal personal fractures and restore pride.

Furthermore, Odimba uses contrasts in language to dramatise the boycott’s effect. Characters who initially accept quiet endurance begin to speak with greater certainty and defiance. Wendell’s shift from boasting and avoidance to rejecting the hustler persona reflects the boycott’s influence in reshaping masculine identity. When he begins to support the movement, it signals that the boycott gives people a new sense of responsibility and belonging. The protest becomes a chance to reclaim pride rather than live in isolation or shame.

In conclusion, Odimba dramatically conveys the impact of the Bristol Bus Boycott by showing how it shapes emotions, relationships and self-worth within a Black British community. Through conflict, transformation, symbolism and structural build-up to collective success, the boycott becomes a powerful force for change.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This response would be placed in the highest band. It offers a confident and sustained exploration of how Odimba dramatically conveys the impact of the bus boycott, keeping a clear focus on how political change is shown through characters, relationships and stagecraft.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The candidate demonstrates secure knowledge of the play, selecting relevant examples involving Princess, Junior, Wendell and Mavis to show how the boycott affects both personal and communal life. The argument is well organised and develops logically, linking the boycott to themes of dignity, belonging and resistance.
> 
> There is strong insight in the way the response engages with Odimba’s dramatic methods. The discussion of dialogue, character conflict, transformation and repeated stage directions shows an understanding of how meaning is created theatrically. The conclusion clearly reinforces the idea that the boycott’s impact is emotional as well as political.
> 
> Overall, this is a perceptive, well-supported and evaluative response that shows strong personal engagement and a mature critical understanding of the play.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Stay focused on the word **“dramatically”** by analysing how the boycott is shown on stage
> - Use **key characters** to explore different impacts (family tension, identity, community unity)
> - Refer to **stage directions and structural build-up** to show dramatic effect
> - Link the boycott to changes in **relationships and self-worth**, not just events
> - Explore **character development**, especially shifts in confidence or responsibility

[*from *Act 1, Scene 1] | |---| How does Odimba make this such an entertaining opening to the play? Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In this opening to Princess & The Hustler, Chinonyerem Odimba makes the scene highly entertaining through lively stagecraft, humour, sharp contrasts and fast-paced dialogue. The audience is immediately drawn into Princess’ imaginative fantasy, before it is suddenly interrupted by Mavis’s practical, no-nonsense parenting. Odimba uses this clash between dream and reality to create comedy, character interest and dramatic tension, making the start of the play memorable and engaging.

Odimba begins with a visually playful stage direction: “The stage opens like a big box — as though opening the front of a doll’s house.” This instantly creates a theatrical sense of fun and invites the audience into a private domestic world. The doll’s house image suggests childhood and make-believe, preparing us for Princess’ imaginative performance. It is entertaining because it feels like we are watching a secret world being revealed.

Princess’ pageant fantasy is presented in a joyful and exaggerated way. She stands “eyes closed” in a “swimming costume and a sash”, placing a crown made of “cardboard and tinsel” on her head. These details are comic because they imitate glamour using cheap, homemade materials. The voice-over heightens the excitement, announcing her as the winner in an inflated tone: “Ladies and gentlemen… [Voice booming] Princess James.” Odimba creates humour by contrasting this grand announcement with the reality of a small “cupboard room”.

The stage directions then turn this private game into a spectacle as the room “explodes into a world of pageantry” filled with “Union Jacks, music and fireworks”. The verb “explodes” suggests sudden energy and visual excitement, making the opening feel vibrant and dramatic. This transformation is entertaining because it feels surprising, like a mini performance within the play, and it shows immediately how powerful Princess’ imagination is.

Princess’ speech is also humorous and charming. She introduces herself formally, “My name is Phyllis Princess James” and promises she will wear her crown “even when I am asleep”, which is comically exaggerated and childlike. Her thanks to her family becomes funny when she adds, “Even though he is so annoying!”, breaking the seriousness of the moment and reminding the audience that this is a child acting out her dream. Odimba also shows Princess’ innocent ambition when she says she will “help the poor” but only after buying her mum “a new coat” and herself “a new bicycle”, creating warmth through her childlike priorities.

The funniest moment arrives when Mavis interrupts, shouting over the noise: “Princess James did you hear what I said?” The sharp shift from fantasy to parental discipline is entertaining because it collapses the pageantry instantly. Mavis’ threat that the next thing Princess will hear is “my hand against your backside” is blunt and exaggerated, capturing the realities of family life in a comic way. The quick exchanges that follow also add energy, as Princess mutters “Beauties of the West” while Mavis pushes her back into chores: “go wash your hands and come help me with the beans.” The contrast between Princess’ dreamy mindset and Mavis’ practicality keeps the opening lively and engaging.

Finally, the entrance of Wendell Junior adds tension and excitement. The detail that “a camera swings around his neck” suggests confidence and style, but Mavis instantly challenges him. Her extreme warning — “You turn the handle of that door and it will be the last thing you do” — creates suspense and makes the audience curious. The “Beat” afterwards holds the tension, leaving the scene on an intriguing cliff-hanger.

In conclusion, Odimba makes this an entertaining opening by combining spectacle with humour and dramatic tension. Princess’ imaginative world creates excitement, Mavis’ interruption adds comedy and realism, and Wendell Junior’s entrance builds suspense, hooking the audience from the start.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This response would be placed in the highest band. It shows a clear and confident understanding of how Odimba makes this opening entertaining, staying closely focused on the question throughout.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The candidate demonstrates secure knowledge of the extract, selecting well-chosen stage directions and quotations to support a sustained analysis. The contrast between Princess’ imaginative fantasy and Mavis’ sharp interruption is explored effectively, showing how humour and energy are created through sudden shifts in tone.
> 
> There is strong insight in the discussion of Odimba’s dramatic methods, particularly spectacle, exaggeration, dialogue and pacing. The essay also recognises how the entrance of Wendell Junior introduces tension and curiosity, helping to hook the audience. Overall, this is a well-structured, perceptive response with clear engagement in how theatre creates entertainment.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Focus on **dramatic methods** such as **stage directions, spectacle and voice-over**
> - Explore the contrast between **fantasy and reality** to show how comedy is created
> - Use **short quotations** to support points about humour and character
> - Comment on **pace and interruptions**, especially Mavis cutting across the pageant
> - Show how Wendell Junior’s entrance creates **tension and anticipation**

(from Act 3, Scene 6) | |---| How does Odimba make this such an inspiring and emotional climax to the play? Remember to support your ideas with details from the text.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

In this extract from Princess & The Hustler, Chinonyerem Odimba creates an inspiring and emotional climax by bringing Princess’ imagination and her longing for affirmation into powerful dramatic focus. Through tenderness, humour, symbolism, and spectacular stagecraft, Odimba transforms the cupboard room into a space where hope becomes real. The scene is emotionally moving because Wendell finally supports Princess in the way she has always needed, and inspiring because Princess’ vision expands into something larger than herself.

Odimba immediately builds emotion through the anticipation and intimacy of Princess calling to her father: “Come out! Come out!” The repetition suggests excitement, but also a child’s desperate desire to be heard. The “Beat” that follows creates a pause of suspense, making the audience wait for Wendell’s response. This silence heightens the emotional intensity because it suggests uncertainty. His appearance is therefore crucial, and Odimba makes it both surprising and uplifting.

Wendell’s entrance is playful and comic, but it also carries emotional weight. He appears “wearing make-up and has a skirt over his trousers”, with a “shawl” and “makeshift headdress”. These costume details are funny, yet they also show Wendell’s willingness to let go of pride and masculinity to make Princess happy. Princess’ delighted reaction, clapping and saying, “Daddy you really look like a real woman…” highlights her innocence and joy. The humour makes the moment warm and affectionate, inviting the audience to share Princess’ excitement rather than judge Wendell. This willingness to play signals emotional change: Wendell is finally engaging as a father.

At the same time, Odimba suggests Wendell’s vulnerability.  When he sees himself in the mirror and pleads, “Lord! Give mi strength!” the comedy is mixed with discomfort. This creates emotional depth, as the audience recognises that Wendell’s participation requires courage. Odimba makes the climax inspiring by showing Wendell  prioritising his daughter.

The emotional power increases as Princess leads Wendell hand in hand into the cupboard room. The stage direction that “The cupboard room is now bigger than it ever looked” symbolises growth and transformation. Earlier in the play, the cupboard represented confinement and hardship, but here it becomes expansive, suggesting freedom and possibility. This physical enlargement reflects Princess’ renewed confidence and Wendell’s growing understanding of her inner world. The pageantry “starts slowly”, building anticipation, like a celebration beginning to awaken.

Wendell’s speechlessness and amazement deepen the emotional impact. His disbelief, “Mi never in mi life see any ting like dis Princess…” , shows genuine admiration rather than mockery. For the first time, Princess is validated by her father. This moment is inspiring because it suggests that love and support can heal earlier neglect, allowing Princess’ imagination to become a shared space rather than a private escape.

Odimba also makes the climax powerful through symbolism. Princess insists, “You have to crown me the winner”, and Wendell agrees, “Every princess need to be crowned far true.” The crowning becomes more than a game. It represents recognition, worth and belonging. When Wendell “gently places the crown” on her head, the tenderness of the action contrasts with his earlier instability, making the gesture feel like a promise of care. The crown symbolises Princess’ ambition, but also her need to be seen as valuable in a world that often devalues her.

Princess’ scripted announcement is another emotional turning point. She instructs Wendell to speak the formal pageant line, and he follows her lead, showing that he is finally listening to her. The moment becomes deeply moving because it reverses the power dynamic: instead of adults controlling children, Princess directs the scene, and Wendell supports her. This makes the climax inspiring because it gives Princess agency and confidence.

The final line — “And now watch everything beautiful in the world come alive…” — is uplifting and poetic, and it triggers the most dramatic stage effect in the extract. The room “explodes into a world of pageantry” with “music and fireworks”, creating a sensory celebration. However, the most emotional detail comes at the end, when Princess imagines “a pageant where all the beauty queens look like her.” This transforms the scene into a moment of empowerment. It suggests that Princess is no longer simply copying a beauty contest that excludes her, but reshaping it into one where she belongs. Odimba makes this inspiring because it celebrates self-recognition and the possibility of change.

In conclusion, Odimba makes this an inspiring and emotional climax through humour, tenderness, symbolism and vivid stage spectacle. Wendell’s participation shows growth and love, while Princess’ expanded imagination becomes a powerful statement of identity and hope. The climax is emotional because it fulfils Princess' need for acceptance, and inspiring because it ends with a vision of beauty that includes and celebrates her.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This response would be placed in the highest band. It offers a confident and perceptive exploration of how Odimba creates an inspiring and emotional climax, maintaining a clear focus on the terms of the question throughout.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The candidate demonstrates secure knowledge of the extract, selecting well-chosen quotations and stage directions to support a sustained analysis. The essay explores how humour, tenderness and spectacle combine to make the scene uplifting, while also recognising the emotional weight of Wendell’s vulnerability and Princess’ longing for affirmation.
> 
> There is strong insight into Odimba’s dramatic methods, particularly the use of costume, pauses, symbolism (the crown), and the staged transformation of the cupboard room. The response also shows clear understanding of why this moment matters structurally, as it completes Princess’ journey and strengthens the play’s message about dignity and belonging. The conclusion effectively reinforces why the climax is both moving and inspiring.
> 
> Overall, this is a well-structured, evaluative and highly engaged response that meets the highest-level criteria.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep a clear focus on **why this moment is both inspiring and emotional**
> - Use **stage directions** to analyse how the climax works in performance
> - Explore how **humour and tenderness** deepen the emotional impact
> - Analyse the symbolism of the **crown/pageant** as recognition and self-worth
> - Comment on how Wendell’s behaviour shows **change and growth**
> - Link the ending to the play’s wider ideas about **identity, belonging and hope**

parts.problemMd:
Read carefully the following poem. The poet describes how the natural world grows back over a town.

**Green Coming**

Give the land one wet season

and see how green come marching back —

vine over the fence, moss on the step,

the old road swallowed soft in leaf.

** **

Nothing here stay still for long.

Bush push up between the paving stones,

lizard flick its blue-quick tongue,

and the guava drop its fruit like small suns

into the long grass, unafraid.

** **

I used to think the town was strong,

its concrete arms, its iron gate —

but concrete crack, and green come through,

patient as a grandmother’s hand

smoothing, smoothing what the years undo.

** **

So let them build their walls up high.

This wild will find the smallest seam,

will root itself in what they leave,

and grow me back a home from air.

By Sonia Alleyne

How does the poet vividly portray the power of the natural world in this poem?

To help you answer this question, you might consider:

- how she makes the green seem alive and unstoppable
- how she contrasts the natural world with the man-made town
- the ways in which the ending connects the natural world to belonging
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

Alleyne shows the natural world as something patient, alive and impossible to stop — a force that lasts longer than anything people build against it.

From the start, the poet makes nature feel active and deliberate. She tells us to “Give the land one wet season / and see how green come marching back”, and the word “marching” shows the green like an army moving forward, sure of itself. Using the single word “green” for the whole living world makes nature seem like one big living thing rather than lots of separate plants. I think this is effective because it makes something we usually see as passive seem like it has its own will. The list that follows — “vine over the fence, moss on the step, / the old road swallowed soft in leaf” — shows nature quietly taking back places people made, and the soft word “swallowed” suggests it does this almost gently.

The poet keeps telling us that nothing human stays still. “Nothing here stay still for long” is short and blunt, almost like a saying, and the Creole grammar — “Bush push up”, “lizard flick” — gives the poem a spoken voice, as if the speaker belongs to this place. The images make the world feel alive: “the lizard flick its blue-quick tongue” is sharp and quick, while the simile “the guava drop its fruit like small suns” makes the fruit sound warm and precious, falling “unafraid” of the town.

The turning point comes when the speaker admits, “I used to think the town was strong, / its concrete arms, its iron gate”. Here the town is given human parts too, but they are cold and hard next to the soft green. The poet then puts the two side by side — “but concrete crack, and green come through” — and the hard ‘c’ sounds in “concrete crack” almost sound like something breaking. The part that moves me most is the simile that nature is “patient as a grandmother's hand / smoothing, smoothing what the years undo”: the repeated “smoothing” slows the line down, and comparing nature to a grandmother links it to family and love, not just survival.

In the last stanza this quiet power turns into a personal statement. “So let them build their walls up high” sounds almost defiant, and the speaker is sure that “This wild will find the smallest seam, / will root itself in what they leave”. The final line — “and grow me back a home from air” — is the most powerful for me: nature does not just take back the land, it seems to grow the speaker a sense of belonging out of nothing. The word “home” makes it personal — the power of the natural world is also the power to give a person a place to belong.

Overall, Alleyne shows the natural world as gentle but impossible to beat. Through personification, the vivid images and the gentle simile of the grandmother, she makes the green feel alive, patient and stronger than concrete. By the end, I don't think the poem is really about plants taking over a town — it is about the quiet strength of belonging, the feeling that nature, and the speaker, will always find a way to grow back.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is a 25-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 8) because it is a sustained, sensitive and detailed response that analyses the poet's methods closely, integrates well-chosen short quotations, and shows a genuine personal engagement with the poem's deeper meaning about resilience and belonging.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The response works through the poem rather than listing devices: it names each method — the personification of “green come marching back”, the guava simile, the Creole voice, the grandmother simile, the contrast of “concrete crack” with the green — and each time explains its effect and links it back to the power of the natural world. Quotations are short and embedded. The reading of the final line as being about belonging, not just plants, shows the individual response and critical understanding expected at the top band. It addresses the intensifier “vividly” throughout and keeps a personal voice (“I think”, “the part that moves me most”) without ever slipping into narrative or losing focus on the writer's methods. As an unseen response it rightly uses no biographical or contextual material.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Track the poem through to the turn at “I used to think the town was strong” — the shift is where the meaning deepens
> - Name the method (personification, simile, contrast) and then explain its effect; do not just spot it
> - Keep quotations short and embedded, and always link them back to the key word in the question — here, “power”
> - Respond to the word “vividly”: show how the poet makes the natural world feel alive
> - Notice what the Creole voice (“green come”, “lizard flick”) adds — a sense of a real speaker and a real place
> - Include a genuine personal response — how the poem makes you feel or what you think it is really about
> - It is an unseen poem, so do not write about the poet's life or context — focus only on close reading

parts.problemMd:
Read carefully the following passage. It is about a girl, Amara, on the morning her family must move out of the only home she has known.

The kettle had already been packed, so her mother boiled water in a saucepan, and they drank the last tea standing up because the chairs were gone.

** **

Amara had not expected the flat to look so large without their things in it. All her life the rooms had felt crowded — the sofa too big, the hallway too narrow for two people to pass — but now, stripped to bare walls and pale rectangles where the pictures had hung, the place seemed to stretch and echo, as if it had been holding its breath for fourteen years and had finally let it out.

** **

She walked from room to room while her mother wrapped the last cups. In the kitchen, a faint brown ring still marked the wall above the cooker, where the steam of a thousand dinners had settled. In the bathroom, her own height was recorded in pencil on the doorframe — a ladder of small lines climbing towards the top, each one dated in her father’s careful hand. She pressed her thumb against the highest mark and felt, absurdly, that if she rubbed hard enough she could keep it.

** **

Outside, a lorry reversed into the courtyard with a long, patient beeping. Men in blue overalls came up the stairs, and the flat that had been so quiet was suddenly full of strangers and the squeal of tape pulled across boxes. Amara stood in the doorway of her bedroom and watched them lift her mattress as though it weighed nothing at all.

** **

“Come and help, love,” her mother said, not unkindly. But Amara could not move. She was looking at the window, at the particular grey square of sky she had woken to every morning, the one crossed by the same television aerial and, in summer, by the swifts that screamed round the rooftops at dusk. She had never thought to wonder where the swifts went when they left. Now she understood that a place could be full of you without your ever noticing, and that you only felt the shape of it when it was taken away.

** **

Her mother came and stood beside her. For a while neither of them spoke. Then her mother said, quietly, “We carry it with us. You’ll see.” She said it the way she said most difficult things — lightly, as if it were nothing — but her hand found Amara’s shoulder and stayed there, warm and certain, and Amara leaned into it without meaning to.

** **

The last box went down. The door of the flat was left open behind them, the way you leave a door open for someone who might still be inside. Amara did not look back. But at the bottom of the stairs, where the light from the courtyard fell across the step, she stopped for just a moment, as though she had heard her name.

How does the writer make you feel about Amara’s experience of leaving her home?

To help you answer this question, you might consider:

- how the writer describes the empty flat and its small details
- how Amara’s thoughts and feelings change as she moves through the rooms
- how the writer makes the final moments so significant
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

The writer makes me feel a deep, quiet sadness for Amara, showing how much it hurts to leave a home so that the loss almost feels physical — but also giving a gentle comfort by the end.

From the start, small ordinary details make the loss feel real. The kettle “had already been packed”, so they drink “the last tea standing up because the chairs were gone”. The phrase “the last tea” makes an everyday thing feel final, and having to stand shows the home is already being taken apart around them. I think this feels honest rather than over the top, because the feeling comes through the objects instead of being stated.

The writer then makes the empty flat seem alive. Stripped bare, “the place seemed to stretch and echo, as if it had been holding its breath for fourteen years and had finally let it out.” This is a powerful bit of personification: the flat is given a body and a breath, so leaving feels like the end of a living relationship. The “pale rectangles where the pictures had hung” are like ghosts of the family’s life, and they made me realise how much of Amara’s past is being wiped away.

As she moves through the rooms, the exact, sensory memories make us feel more sympathy. The “faint brown ring” left by “the steam of a thousand dinners” puts years of family life into one small stain, while the pencil height-marks “each one dated in her father’s careful hand” show her whole childhood. When she presses her thumb to “the highest mark” and feels that “if she rubbed hard enough she could keep it”, the writer shows how much she wants to hold on; the word “absurdly” shows she knows it is impossible, which makes it sadder.

The removal men make the loss feel worse by contrast. The flat “was suddenly full of strangers and the squeal of tape”, and the harsh word “squeal” breaks the tender mood. Watching them “lift her mattress as though it weighed nothing at all” is really sad in a quiet way — to them it is just an object, but to her it is part of her life — and her stillness, when “she could not move”, shows how overwhelmed she is.

The ending is made important by a change towards understanding and comfort. Looking at “the particular grey square of sky” and the swifts that “screamed round the rooftops at dusk”, Amara realises “a place could be full of you without your ever noticing… you only felt the shape of it when it was taken away.” This feels true to me. But the writer does not leave her alone in her sadness: her mother’s hand “found Amara’s shoulder and stayed there, warm and certain”, and the simple words “We carry it with us” give real comfort. The last image — Amara stopping “as though she had heard her name” — is sad and hopeful at the same time, as if the home is calling to her even as she leaves.

Overall, the writer makes me feel Amara’s loss strongly through personification, small tender details and the way the passage moves from sadness to comfort. By the end I feel that leaving a home is not just losing a place but carrying it inside you — and that Amara, held by her mother, will do exactly that.

parts.problemMd:
Read carefully the following poem, in which the speaker notices himself becoming like his father.

**Spit**

It starts with the small things. The way

I check the locks twice, then a third time,

back door, front door, the bolt on the shed,

same circuit he walked every night of his life.

** **

I’ve got his hands now — the same blunt thumbs,

the nail he lost to a car door in ’91

grown back wrong on me too, somehow,

though that was his door, his decade, not mine.

** **

I say his sayings without meaning to.

“We’ll see.” “Money doesn’t grow on trees.”

The words come up like water from a well

I never knew I’d sunk, or he’d dug first.

** **

For years I swore I’d not turn out like him.

Now here I am, at the mirror, half-past six,

shaving the exact same patch I always miss —

and there he is, looking back, missing it too.

By Neil Sowerby

How does the poet vividly convey the speaker’s feelings about becoming like his father?

To help you answer this question, you might consider:

- how the poet shows the father’s habits appearing in the speaker
- the speaker’s changing attitude across the poem
- how the ending makes this moment so striking
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

Sowerby vividly conveys the speaker’s mixed feelings about turning into his father — a slow, almost frightened realisation that moves from resistance to a kind of sad acceptance.

At the start, the poet shows the change creeping in through tiny habits. “It starts with the small things. The way / I check the locks twice, then a third time” — the flat, everyday opening makes the feeling ordinary and real, and the list of “back door, front door, the bolt on the shed” shows the speaker copying his father’s exact routine, “same circuit he walked every night of his life”. I think the word “same” is important here, because it shows the speaker noticing he has become a copy without ever choosing to.

The poet then makes the inheritance physical. The speaker says “I’ve got his hands now — the same blunt thumbs, / the nail he lost to a car door in ’91 / grown back wrong on me too, somehow”. The specific detail of the lost nail makes it feel true, and the idea that his father’s old injury has “grown back wrong on me too” suggests the speaker has inherited not just habits but damage, as if the past has printed itself onto his body. This makes his feelings seem uneasy — he is watching himself become someone else.

The speaker’s discomfort grows when he hears his father in his own voice. “I say his sayings without meaning to. / ‘We’ll see.’ ‘Money doesn’t grow on trees.’” The ordinary phrases show how deep the inheritance goes, and the simile that “The words come up like water from a well / I never knew I’d sunk, or he’d dug first” is the cleverest moment in the poem. It suggests the father’s influence is buried deep inside the speaker, and that he is drawing on it without realising, which makes becoming his father feel unavoidable rather than chosen.

The turning point is when the speaker admits how he used to feel. “For years I swore I’d not turn out like him. / Now here I am” — the short, blunt sentence “Now here I am” shows the gap between what he wanted and what has happened, and I feel there is a quiet defeat in it. He has lost the argument with himself.

The ending is what makes the poem so striking. The speaker is “at the mirror, half-past six, / shaving the exact same patch I always miss — / and there he is, looking back, missing it too.” The poet saves the biggest moment for the last line, and it works because the father appears in the mirror as the speaker’s own reflection. It is sad and a little funny at the same time — the small failure of missing the same patch of stubble becomes proof that the two men are, in the end, the same person. The word “there” makes it feel as if the father is really present, alive in the speaker’s face.

Overall, Sowerby conveys the speaker’s feelings as a mixture of resistance, unease and, finally, acceptance. Through the everyday habits, the physical detail of the hands, the simile of the well and the reflection in the mirror, he shows a man realising he has become his father — and by the end I feel that this is something the speaker has stopped fighting, even if he is not quite happy about it.

This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 8) because it analyses the poet’s methods closely, traces the speaker’s changing feelings across the whole poem, uses short embedded quotations, and shows a personal, critical understanding of the poem’s deeper idea about inheritance.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The response follows the speaker’s feelings from resistance to acceptance rather than listing techniques: it reads the flat, everyday opening, the physical inheritance of the hands and nail, the well simile, and the mirror image, and each time explains the effect and how it conveys the speaker’s mixed feelings. Quotations are short and well chosen. The reading of the final line — the father appearing as the speaker’s own reflection — is precise and shows the individual response expected at the top band. It addresses “vividly” throughout and never drifts into narrative.

parts.problemMd:
Read carefully the following passage. A girl, Nadia, stands on a high diving board for the first time.

The ladder had seemed like nothing from the ground.

** **

Nadia had watched the others go up it all afternoon, one after another, stepping off the high board as easily as walking through a door, and she had thought: I can do that. But the ladder was longer than it looked, and the higher she climbed the more the rungs seemed to narrow under her wet feet, until she reached the top and the board stretched out in front of her, white and dry and utterly still, over a very long way of nothing.

** **

She walked to the end of it because there was nowhere else to go. Behind her, someone was already climbing. Below, the pool had shrunk to a bright blue rectangle, and the people around it had become small and busy and far away, their voices flattened by distance into a single soft roar, like the sea heard through a shell. A breeze she had not felt on the ground moved across her arms and lifted the hairs there one by one.

** **

She looked down. That was the mistake. The water, which had looked soft and welcoming from below, now looked hard as a tabletop, a flat blue lid over something she could not see the bottom of. Her toes curled over the rough edge of the board. Her heart was doing something complicated and painful against her ribs, and her legs had turned to something that was not quite bone.

** **

“Whenever you’re ready,” a voice called up, kind and bored at the same time, the voice of someone who had said it a thousand times.

** **

But that was the trouble. She would never be ready. There was no version of this where she felt ready. She understood, standing there with the whole blue afternoon holding its breath around her, that being ready was not a thing that arrived; it was a thing you decided, or didn’t. You either stepped off the edge of the ordinary world, or you turned round and climbed back down the ladder past all the waiting faces, and lived.

** **

Somewhere far below, her little brother was watching. She could not see him but she knew he was, the way you always know. He thought she could do anything. It was the most annoying and the most necessary thing about him.

** **

Nadia closed her eyes. She thought of nothing. And then, before the part of her that wanted to live could stop her, she let her weight tip forward into the empty air —

How does the writer create a sense of tension in this passage?

To help you answer this question, you might consider:

- how the writer describes what Nadia sees and feels on the board
- how the writer uses the people around her to build the tension
- how the ending leaves you feeling
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer

The writer builds a strong sense of tension by making us feel every moment of Nadia’s fear on the high board, and by holding back the ending so we are left, like her, on the edge.

The writer creates tension straight away by contrasting how easy the dive looked with how frightening it becomes. “The ladder had seemed like nothing from the ground” is a short, blunt opening, but it sets up the gap between watching and doing. When Nadia climbs, “the rungs seemed to narrow under her wet feet”, and the detail of the “wet feet” makes us imagine slipping, which adds to the fear. The board is described as “white and dry and utterly still, over a very long way of nothing”, and the phrase “a very long way of nothing” makes the empty air below feel huge and threatening.

The writer then uses what Nadia sees to build the tension. The pool “had shrunk to a bright blue rectangle” and the people “had become small and busy and far away”, which shows how high up she is and how alone she feels. The simile that their voices are “flattened by distance into a single soft roar, like the sea heard through a shell” is effective, because it cuts her off from everyone below and makes the moment feel strange and dreamlike. Even the “breeze she had not felt on the ground” adds to the sense that she has entered a different, more dangerous world.

The most tense moment comes when she looks down. “That was the mistake” is a short sentence that lands like a warning. The water “now looked hard as a tabletop, a flat blue lid over something she could not see the bottom of”, and this simile is frightening because it turns something soft into something solid and deadly. The writer then makes the fear physical: “Her heart was doing something complicated and painful against her ribs, and her legs had turned to something that was not quite bone.” I think describing her legs like this is clever, because it shows she is losing control of her own body.

The people around her make the tension worse. The instructor’s voice is “kind and bored at the same time”, and the fact that he has said it “a thousand times” reminds us that this is huge for Nadia but nothing to him, which makes her feel even more alone. Her little brother, watching from below, adds pressure too, because “he thought she could do anything” — she does not want to let him down, and this raises what is at stake.

The ending is where the writer uses tension most cleverly. Nadia realises “being ready was not a thing that arrived; it was a thing you decided”, and then “before the part of her that wanted to live could stop her, she let her weight tip forward into the empty air —”. The writer ends on a dash, right at the moment she jumps, so we never see her hit the water. This leaves the tension unresolved and holds us in the same frightening moment as Nadia. I found this a powerful way to end, because the fear is left hanging in the air, exactly like she is.

Overall, the writer creates tension through the contrast between watching and doing, the frightening images of the water and the height, the physical description of Nadia’s fear, and the unresolved ending. By stopping at the very moment of the jump, the writer makes us feel the tension of the leap without ever letting it go.

> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The question is about atmosphere, so the response keeps its focus on how tension is made: the contrast between watching and doing, the frightening similes (“hard as a tabletop”, “like the sea heard through a shell”), the physical description of fear, the isolating instructor and the watching brother, and the dash that ends the passage mid-jump. Each point names a method and explains its effect on the reader. Quotations are short and never become retelling. The reading of the unresolved ending as leaving the reader “on the edge” shows the evaluative, personal response expected at the top band.
